speechtext: Yes.

I see in the Estimates,
item 128 "Public buildings; Ottawa Parlia-

merit Buildings," etc. In the column 192021 you ask for $2,000,000 and then coming immediately after the last item there is
Appropriations not required
for 1920-21	$1,000,000 ,
Which shows that in 1919-20 there had been expended, appropriated, credited or charged to the total of $3,000,000 this amount of $1,000,000 and it would only leave $1,000,000 to be expended in 1920-21.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The $2,000,000 that we are voting now is for the Parliament Buildings alone. In last year's Estimates there was an item of $1,000,000 for buildings other than the Parliament Buildings that we are dropping this year as we do not propose to proceed with the work.

That is not an explanation. You are asking Parliament to vote money for:
Ottawa Parliament Building-Restoration- the plans for the said building and the method to be adopted for securing the reconstruction thereof to be subject to the approval of the joint committee appointed by the Prime Minister and the leader of the Opposition, $2,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes.
You have in the column 1920-21, $2,000,000. You say there: "W; are asking for $2,000,000 but we do not want the $2,000,000; we just want $1,000,000," as $1,000,000 voted in 1919-20 was not required.

That was for
other buildings and it is not proposed to expend it this year.
You charge it as having been expended last year.
No.
Why does it come in the column for 1919-20?

My hon. friend
will see that it - is put in the column for 1919-20 because it was voted for 1919-20. But
1919-	20 has passed and the million has not been expended on these other buildings. Therefore it shows that the amount was voted last year and that it is not being voted this year.
I may be defective in my understanding of the English language but in one year you say that an amount of $1,000,000 is not required while you are asking for $2,000,000 for the years 1920-21.
That is right.

But you say that the appropriation of $1,000,000 is not required for
1920-	21.

That is merely to carry out the comparison. If that $1,000,000 was not carried out in that column it would appear as if the $1,000,000 which was voted last year had been used. To make it plain, and according to the truth, that column shows you two things, first, that it was voted last year but that it was not used last year and that therefore it has lapsed.
If it was voted last year why do you keep the column in the Estimates headed "Revote"? If it was not expended last year why not put it in the first column as a revote of $1,000,000?

Because it is not proposed to use the $1,000,000 for the purpose for which that money was appropriated last year. That $1,000,000 was appropriated last year for a certain purpose but it was not used. This year is one in which economy is to be practised and it is not proposed to use the $1,000,000; therefore it goes into the unappropriated column. The appropriation of last year is not being carried over into this year.
I am not satisfied with the explanation.
Sleep over it.

/No, I will not sleep over it; I will get it through my head before I go to bed if it is possible to do so from the very muddy explanation which I have got. Last year you did not expend $1,000,000 which was voted for the Parliament Buildings? Is that the statement you made?

No, the statement I made was that this $1,000,000 was appropriated for public buildings other than these Parliament Buildings. The appropriation voted last year was not used. If we proposed to use it again this year this $1,000,000 would appear in the column for 1920-21 as a re-vote. Then you would have a re-vote and consequently $1,000,000 more to be expended this year.
That makes the case worse.
I give it up.
According to the right hon. gentleman's statement, in 1919-20 you spent only $1,000,000 instead of $2,000,000. Is that right?
No.
You appropriated '$2,000,000.
I do not know how much was appropriated for general public buildings but I do know that $1,000,000 was not spent.
You ask for $2,000,000 this year?
Yes.
Why do. you ask for that when it is not required?
We do not.
You do; you say that $1,000,000 was not required and you ask us to vote $2,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Perhaps I can explain it. Last year, in the Estimates for 1919-20 we voted $2,000,000 to be expended on the Parliament Buildings, then we voted $1,000,000 as well to be spent on~ other buildings. We spent the $2,000,000 on the Parliament Buildings and that left the other $1,000,000 which we did not spend. That $1,000,000 was not used and of course we put it in here in the column headed "191920" to show that although it was voted last year we are not voting anything for these buildings this year. We are asking for $2,000,000 to be expended on these buildings in 1920-21. The $2,000,000 voted for the Parliament Buildings for 1919-20 was expended.

I conclude that we have printed on this page of the Estimates something that is absolutely useless except to give the Government an opportunity of coming to us and saying that last year they came to us and asked us to vote $1,000,000 for which they had no use and which they have not expended.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I think the explanation is this: The Estimates have been made out this year the same as in every previous year. Take an item which appears on the opposite side of the book. Hon. gentlemen will see "Chambly-Improvements in the canals." Last year we voted $40,000. This year we ask $17,000. The statement shows that we spent $23,000 and we are asking for $17,000. The votes of 1919-20 are there so that the committee will have before it a statement of the amount voted last year so as to 'be able to compare with the sum we are voting this year. The items which were not used in 1919-20 and will not be required this year will not appear in the Estimates for 1920-21.

If the appropriations are not required for 1920-21 I do not see what

is the use of having them appear. Unless by keeping the amounts there it is desired to fool the committee to the extent of a few millions, I do not see what is the use of having these items appear when they are not required.

Can my hon. friend point to any single instance during the regime of the late Administration or that of the present Government where the items weTe not shown exactly as. they appear here? My hon. friend is trying to make a lot of wool out of nothing.

The hon. gentleman forgets that this is a period of reconstruction and improvement-we even want to improve the voices of members, their hearing, and the acoustics of the Chamber. It is high time that there should be improvement made with respect to these Estimates so that it should be made abundantly clear to members what is meant, and thus save a lot of discussion about it.

I wish to ask a question which has weighed very heavily on the minds of a large number of people. It will be remembered that in the conflagration which destroyed the former Parliament Buildings, the library was saved by the prompt closing of the iron doors at the entrance to it by one of the attendants. The fire, which was close at hand, was prevented from getting into the library and no damage was done there. However, the fire extended in. other directions, tongues of flame as long as two hundred feet being developed by the great draught. Now it has appeared to some people that if there had been iron doors on the corridors in other parts of the building at least two-thirds of the structure would have been saved as well as valuable lives. It may be said that the present building is fireproof. Well, the wood in it is not, nor is the furniture, and should a fire start very great damage might be done as in the case of the old buildings. Has the simple expedient of having iron doors in any of the corridors, the same as at the Library, been adopted?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
No provision, as I understand, has been made for iron doors in the present building. We are assured that the building is absolutely fireproof, except with respect to the wood in the Chamber, so that in case of fire its effects would be localized. The old building, of course, was not fireproof. Had fireproof doors been provided in different sections of the old build-

ing there might not have been such destruction of property. However, no provision has been made for -such a thing as the hon. gentleman has mentioned.
What about safeguards against smoke? Smoke would smother anybody running through these halls.
Is there any provision in this vote for supplying furniture for the new building?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Furniture is included in the total cost of the construction of the building. We have ordered some and intend ordering more. The cost will come out of this vote for $2,000,000.
A part of this vote may be used for the purchase of furniture for the building?	,

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes.
Who has charge of the purchase of the furniture?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
That is done through
the committee which is supervising the work of construction. The officials of the Public Works Department call for tenders in the ordinary way and submit those tenders to the committee appointed for the purpose of awarding contracts and looking after the construction of the building.
Are tenders for furniture required in the different departments of this building now being called for?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: No tenders have as yet been called for- I am informed that the nature of the permanent furniture to be placed in the building has not yet been decided. The committee is still considering the question before it calls for tenders.

Has the Public Works
Department, or the Supervising Committee, any say in the fixing of the wages paid to the employees by the contractors?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The Labour Department generally decides questions of that kind. In the event of a dispute the Labour Department is called in and whatever they say is a fair wage to be paid is paid by the contractors.

Is all the work being done by the one contractor? For instance, have Lyall and Sons provided the heating apparatus and plumbing as well as the other work?
911	.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The Lyall Company are the contractors for everything in connection with the building.

Does the committee to which the minister referred really exist? At one time it did but is it still in existence? If so I do not think it meets very often. I am not complaining, because I think this expenditure is one for which the Government must take the responsibility. The minister states that tenders are being called for the furniture by the committee, whereas the committee in my opinion meets very seldom. Practically it is not a working committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I do not agree with the hon. member. The Deputy Minister of Public Works tells me that there have been fifty-seven meetings of the committee and in nearly every case those meetings have been fairly well attended.
Who compose the committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: At the present time, Mr. Ballantyne, Mr. Calder, Sir James Loug-heed, Senator Robertson, Senator Watson and myself-six.

There are very few
Liberals on it.

Senator Watson seems to be in excellent company; it is a case of five to one. During the recess I do not imagine the committee is able to meet frequently. .When Parliament is in session it can of course meet more regularly, four or five of these gentlemen being members of the Government. I am not complaining of the infrequent meetings-I think this is an expenditure for which the Government must be responsible-but I do not regard this a working committee out of session.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I must take issue with the hon. gentleman and tell him that Senator Watson comes all the way from Manitoba to Ottawa to attend the meetings of the committee.

That is a long way
to come.	,

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
When the Hon. Mr. Pugsley was a member of the committee he also came from St. John to attend meetings of the committee. Those meetings have all been well attended and all its members have taken a deep interest in everything connected with the construction of the building. I can assure the hon. member that the committee are called together quite

often and always consider these tenders as they are submitted.
The committee at present is composed of five ministers and Senator Watson; is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That is so.
That is rather lopsided.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: We would be very glad to re-organize it.
I do not complain.
Has anything been settled about the tower yet?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
We had a meeting of
the committee a few days' ago. A working model is being prepared, but nothing has been finally decided as yet.
Has the minister considered the question of installing chimes in the tower?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Not yet,
Has the committee yet considered tenders for silverware and cutlery for the restaurant?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The matter was before the committee recently. Two tenders were received,-one from Mappin & Webb, and the other from Cassidy & Sons.
Which tender was accepted?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Cassidy's tender was
the lower, and we accepted it, as in all cases.
As in all cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes, the lowest tender is usually accepted.
Is the present furniture of this Chamber to be considered as permanent, or is any particular committee paying attention to the colour scheme of the decoration?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The desks now installed, with the exception of the front row, are supposed to be permanent, but the chairs are only temporary.
How many architects are now connected with the enterprise?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Two; Mr. PeaTson and Mr. Marchand,-the same two who originally took the contract.
Will the minister tell us when may we expect carpets in our offices?

Order. Mr. McCrea
has the floor.	j,

This vote of $2,000,000 I
presume will have to be granted, because the building must be completed, but I would like to ask the minister or the committee in charge of this worji whether it would not be possible to speed it up a little? During the past couple of months I have had opportunities of occasionally watching what was going on, and I think it would be wise for those in charge tb see that at least we get a little work done right here under the eyes of the country's representatives, for the money we are paying. If the committee have not already done so, I would advise them to look around where Lyall and other contractors are doing work on a contract rather than a percentage basis and see if there is not a little difference in the speed with which operations are conducted under contract. One need not be very observant to notice the sluggish movements of the men on this job-in fact, it is really amusing to see how they proceed with their work. For instance, I saw one big husky man the other day going through the performance of scrubbing floors. The charwoman gets on her knees and does the same work expeditiously and efficiently. This man was sitting down at the job, and although I do not know what rate of pay he was receiving, it struck me as a rather expensive way of doing that class of work, and if all the other work is being conducted along the same lines I think it would be well for the committee to take steps to speed up the men in charge.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Might it not be possible that the man my hon. friend refers to is lame and cannot use his legs?
He had not any appearance of being lame. I think he was more lazy than lame.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The question has been before the committee several times, and we are doing everything we can to speed up the work and get it completed before next session.

If the man my hon. friend from Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea) refers to was a returned soldier with a lame leg, I would be the last man to interfere with him, as I am sure my hon. friend would be. He may look all right, but after being at the front he may have legs which are of little avail to him notwithstanding his husky appearance. I think my hon. friend should find out whether the man he is complaining about is not a returned soldier with a wooden leg.

,Mr. DENIS: The point which has just been raised by the hon. member for Sherbrooke gives us an inkling of the wrong principle upon which the contract for this building was let. We have been told that the contractors receive a certain percentage on $5,000,000. Over and above the $5,000,000 mark I would ask the minister what interest have the contractors in reducing the expense? Are the contractors, or is 'Re minister, or the committee, or any one else in this House or in the country interested in seeing that the money of the people is properly expended? If the cost runs to $10,000,000 or $12,000,000 or $15,000,000, what would it matter to the contractors? They do not care, they are here on the job, and, if the representations made by the member for Sherbrooke are correct, they let the men work just as they please. I think this is a very pertinent question for the attention of the minister: whether any one is interested in seeing that this work is being conducted efficiently and in a way that every dollar spent will bring to the country a dollar's worth of work.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

No.
%
My question was qurte plain.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I was just speaking to the deputy minister.

My point is this, briefly: Is anybody interested in seeing that this money is being properly expended? It is clear that the contractors have no interest in reducing the expenditure. When a man contracts to do a piece of work he is interested in seeing that the money is properly expended because he is paying out that money. Who is paying the money in this particular case? The managers of the contractors are looking after the work, but no one is interested in seeing that the work is properly done and the money not spent improvidently.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: My hon. friend does not understand the situation or he would not make that statement. In the first place, we have two first-class architects in charge of this work-Mr. Pearson and Mr. Mar-chand.
How are they paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: By commission.
Are they interested in reducing the cost of the work?

Men of their reputation I should think would be interested in seeing that the cost was kept down to the minimum. But in addition to that, when this work was started we took Mr. Ewart, the Chief Engineer of the Public Works Department-
The Chief Architect.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes.-and in my opinion he is one of the most reliable men ever employed in the Civil Service. We placed him here as representing the Government, and he has been on this work exclusively since the contract was given. We have in addition three first class inspectors who are around the building all the time seeing that the work is properly done.
What are their names?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Mr. Sutherland, Mr. Keefer and Mr. Clancy. These men see that the work is properly done and pressed to completion as fast as possible. They report to the deputy minister. Mr. Ewart also appears before the Committee at intervals and informs them how the work is progressing. He told us at a meeting of the Committee the other day that the work was not progressing as fast as he would like, and we are taking measures accordingly.
The minister stated just now that the cost of the building would be $10,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Roughly.

And $7,000,000 has been expended. The first estimate was for $5,000,000. Alight I ask on what that estimate was based? The increase seems rather strange, because the estimate was made during the war and therefore the difference between pre-war and after-the-war prices can hardly be alleged as the reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The original estimate ol $5,000,000 was made by Mr. Pearson and Mr. Lyall. Since that estimate was made the increased cost of material and labour accounts for a further $2,000,000 at least.

That still leaves $3,000,000 to be accounted for. According to the minister, the original estimate of $5,000,000 has been increased by $2,000,000 because of the increased cost of material and labour, and we are now told that the ultimate cost will be $10,000,000. That still leaves $3,000,000 to play upon.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals

speechtext: It is very hard for us to understand this increase, too.
Does this vote include the supplying of heat to the Western Block, the Post Office, the Eastern Block, and the Langevin Block?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: This vote includes the power-house and the tunnelling.
Is the cost of that charged to the Parliament Building?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes.

I think we should know how much the Parliament Building itself has cost outside of this other work. I have been over this tunnelling and heating plant, and I know it is very expensive work, because that happens to be my trade. I do not think the cost should he included in the Parliament Building costs. There is an awful draft playing around the seats to the left of the Speaker's chair. I wish the minister would bring this to the attention of the architects, because at present the seats cannot be occupied when the door is open.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I will bring that matter to their attention.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I shall be very glad to get the figures my hon. friend desires. I am informed by the deputy minister that the power-house and the main tunnel will cost in the neighbourhood of half a million dollars. That is charged to this building although the plant heats the other buildings as well.

The main tunnel is
charged to this building?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes. To connect the Eastern Block, the Langevin Block, the Western Block, and the Supreme Court, has cost about $35,000.
Is the Hunter Block connected to this system?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: No. The deputy minister informs me that the $35,000 is not all charged to the Parliament Building, but I will give the exact figures later.

We have already voted $2,000,000 for the completion of this building, and those are only two of the many millions which are in the Estimates for the Department of Public Works. That just shows the importance of having at the head of the department a man who can devote his whole time to its business. My hon. friend is very active, but he has his own department to supervise.
And the game to play.
I think it is only fair that the country should have the benefit of a full-fledged Minister of Public Works.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Will you take the job?
Not in this Government.
That might be the only way for this Government to get a minister re-elected.

It may be due to my lack of progressiveness that I find my office and those of several others on the same floor absolutely unprepared for living in when -we come here. Some furniture is required, and although I have repeatedly asked for some provision to be made, even temporarily, in the way of a filing cabinet and a hatraek for my hat and coat, I have been .unable to procure those very necessary articles of furniture. I have been informed that elaborate desks and filing cabinets will . eventually be provided, and in the meantime we shall manage with desks without locks and so forth. But some temporary arrangements might be made in the offices of new members who have not any of these

modern conveniences, or, one might say, any conveniences at all, so that we could carry on in the meantime. I should like something in which to file away some of the volumes of stuff I am gathering around in corners on the floor, and something on which to hang my hat and coat, instead of having to set them down on the couch.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The complaint made by the hon. member (Mr. Verville) about the draught, is the first complaint of that nature we have had and I will draw the attention of the architect to the matter..
If my hon. friend (Mr. Gould) thinks any furniture or anything else is required in his room to make it comfortable for carrying on his work, all he has to do is to make a requisition on the Serjeant-at-Arms who will see that the matter is attended to at once. If that requisition is not carried out, if the hon. member will drop me a line, I will see that the matter is attended to immediately.
Mr. MAHARiG:	Is that statement supposed to have general application?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The Serjeant-at-Arms has charge of the building, and if anything is necessary, he makes the application. If he thinks a requisition is unreasonable, he may submit it to the Department of Public Works for approval.

I suppose due regard
will be had to what are the modest demands of the members of the Farmers' Party.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes.

I have adopted that procedure on three or four occasions, and I am sure the Serjeant-at-Arms has done his best on behalf of the members who are on that floor; but apparently stocks are not available, and I should like to know what procedure is being taken to get them.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I will make inquiries of the Serjeant-at-Arms as to what requisitions he has that have not been filled, and we shall try to have them filled at the earliest possible moment.

Five or six months ago
tenders were called for the supplying of desks and other furniture of rooms throughout the building; tenders were put in, and I think contracts were practically decided upon when some objection was found with the nature of the desks, it being considered that they were of too expensive a quality and so on. The matter was supposed to come before the Government, and I should like to know what has been done with regard
to it and what disposition has been made of the tenders. Is there any likelihood of contracts being awarded, or is the matter to be left open for another five or six months?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The chief architect prepared designs for desks and tenders were called. The cost of the desks amounted to $180 each, but the committee thought they were too expensive and that another design should be made that would, perhaps, answer the purpose and at the same time be more economical. We have asked the chief architect to submit new designs, but up to the present time he has not had time to prepare them. We had the matter up at the last committee meeting, and we expect to have the designs within a short time, when we shall be ready to call for tenders.
Have the original tenderers been informed that their tenders are not to be considered further?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes, and their checks have been returned.

I wish to call the minister's attention to the following fact. When we address the House in English, we have a very convenient and comfortable room where we can go and look at the stenographer's notes and correct whatever errors and mistakes may have slipped in; but on the other hand, if we speak in French and we wish to correct our speeches, the French stenographers are in a room with everybody else, with about twenty-five typewriters working, so that it is absolutely impossible for one to do any work. I understand that, as the original plans for the disposition of rooms stood, the French stenographers were given a separate room where the 5 p.m. French members could have gone to do their work. But for some reason or another instructions were given by somebody whose name I do not know; two gentlemen were put into that separate room, and the French stenographers were put into that large room I mentioned with about twenty-five or thirty other people. This is a great inconvenience, and it surely should be sufficient to draw the attention of the minister to the fact to obtain an immediate remedy.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I understand that the rooms of this building are all under the direction of the Speaker and not of the Minister of Public Works. I will draw the Speaker's attention to the statement made by the hon. member, but from what I can understand the room that is intended for

the French stenographers is under construction and not yet completed.
They had one and it was taken away from them.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: All I can say is that I will draw the attention of the Speaker to the matter and see that it is remedied.
I trust the minister will use his influence to remedy it.
Is it the intention of this joint committee to spend any of this $2,000,000 in improving the library?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That matter has not as yet come before the committee which has so far been dealing with the main building. If any improvement or other work is necessary in connection with the library, it will have to be done, and it would be included in any moneys expended in connection with the construction of this building.

If the minister goes to
the library-and I am sure he goes there often-he will notice that books are stacked in the shelves four and five layers deep so that it is absolutely impossible to find any books, and papers are stored away in files so that we cannot find what we want; in fact, most of the books are in the cellars. It is very important that this committee should look after that part of the building and see that proper accommodation is given so that the books will be displayed in such a way that the members can find the books they require.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I will look into the
matter.
Does the architect receive a commission on the furnishings as well as on the construction of the building?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: No arrangement was made with the architects with reference to the furniture, but I think they are entitled to a commission on that as well as on the building. They are the ones who are designing the furniture, calling for tenders and so on.
What is the rate of commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Five and one-half per cent,

Will that be on the
$10,000,000 estimate?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals

speechtext: Is there any arrangement for any commission to be paid after the $5,000,000 has been exceeded?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals

speechtext: Then, the Government do not intend paying any additional fees to the architects over and above an expenditure of $5,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: We have not considered anything other than the contract up to the present time.

What authority has this
joint committee of senators and members of the House? Does it merely supervise the construction, or has it power to let contracts, or are all contracts subject to the approval or supervision of the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The committee got its authority from a resolution passed by the House authorizing the appointment of this committee, and it, not the Department of Public Works, has power to award contracts and to carry on the work.

,Are these contracts not subject to revision by the Government itself? II ask this question because of the contract to which I referred a little while ago in connection with tenders for desks.
I think the committee had approved of what the architect had designed and had practically awarded the contract; but the Government stepped in, I understand, and nullified the whole thing. Just how much power has this committee? Or is everything subject to revision by the Government afterwards?
'Mr. J. D. RETD: The architects submitted plans for the furniture and the committee approved of them and called for tenders. But the tenders amounted to so much more than the sum which the committee thought we should pay for desks that it was decided not to accept them. It was not the Government but the committee that refhsed to accept the tenders.
;Mr. EULER: Had the committee the actual power to do so?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Yes, the committee has power to accept tenders and award contracts. Minutes are made of each meeting,

showing the tenders that have been received, and unless the committee passes on a contract it is not awarded.
How often does the committee meet?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: There have been sixty-seven meetings since the building operations commenced. [I cannot say from memory how often we meet each year, but we meet frequently.
Who compose the committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I gave that information a few moments ago.

A short while ago the minister gave an answer that seems to me to be evasive, and II should like to get some definite information from him. The question was asked as to whether the architects were receiving five and a half per cent up to five million dollars, or five and a half per cent on the whole amount expended, and the minister said: "As we understand it, it was five and a half per cent up to five millions." The minister must surely be in possession of sufficient knowledge to give a more precise and satisfactory statement than this.
Mr. J.*D. REID: We made a contract with Lyall whereby they were to receive five and a half per cent up to five million dollars.
I am speaking of the architects.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The agreement with
them was that we should pay five and a half per cent up to five million dollars. The work has cost a great deal more. Mr. Pearson thinks he is underpaid, and there the matter stands; but there is no question legally but that all we have to pay is five and a half per cent up to five million dollars.
Mr. VERVTLIlEi:	How much has been
paid to Mr. Pearson and Mr. Marchand? What will they receive on the furniture?
, Mr. REID: The two architects made an agreement limiting the amount of expenditure at the time to five million dollars.
That was the cost of the building at the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
That was what they estimated would be the cost of the building. The matter of the furniture was not discussed at the time, but as I have stated,
they will be entitled to something on that as well. Mr. Pearson claims that he will not be able to come out square on the agreement.
Do they receive anything for the plans?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
No; it is included in the commission they receive.
Mr. DuTREMBLAY: Was a tender called for at the outset for the entire building?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
No.
Mr. DuTREMBLAY:	What portion of
work has been given to (Lyall?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The whole work; that is, on a percentage basis,
Mr. DuTREMBLAY: That is probably ihp reason why this building has cost so much, and why its erection has been so protracted. Every practical builder knows that this method is the longest way in construction. Every day that this building remains unfinished means a certain cost to the public, and I think that the committee henceforth should change its method.
Are the furnishings included in the estimate of ten million dollars, or does this sum represent the building alone?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The estimate of ten million dollars includes the building and the necessary furniture.

What proportion of this amount will represent expenditures on furnishings?
Mr, J. D. RETD: Half a million, I understand.
I suppose the ten millions include the cost of the tower.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Everything.

In connection with the item for architects' commission, >1 put on the Order Paper a few days ago a question in reply to which I received the information that up to the 28th day of April, 1919, the architects had been paid $255,354.24. Now, apparently, from what the minister tells us, after that payment on the 28th of April, 1919, up to the present time, a period of nearly one year, no payment has been made to the architects on account of the work done during that time. As I understand, they have been employed continuously during the whole year. It seems to me that this committee, to whom is entrusted the

supervision of the building and the expending of this large amount of ten million dollars, have not been careful in their duties, or they would have had some definite arrangement with the architects since the 28th of April, 1919. My hon. friend says that Mr. Pearson alleges that he has not been adequately paid, and makes a claim upon the committee for a further sum. If it was necessary at the beginning of the construction of this building that the committee should have a clear understanding of the contract under which the architect was to receive 51 per cent on an expenditure of $5,000,000, it is certainly necessary that we should have a clear understanding of what we are proposing to pay the architect for the completion of the building and the purchase of furniture which is to be entrusted to him. We are asked to vote $2,000,000 for the completion of the building.
Mr. MARlCIL: Towards the completion of the building?

Yes, towards the completion of the building. The minister has control of the Department of Public Works which has the supervision and control of this building it is the duty of the minister and the Government to come before the House and definitely and conclusively tell us how much is to be paid the architect and the other officials who are carrying on this work.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I thought the hon. gentleman had that information in the answer to the question as to the amount which has been paid to the architects. The amount is $255,000 and $275,000 would be the total.
There will be $19,000 more to pay?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Yes. The architects
are complaining that the amount they agreed to is not ^sufficient, and they are asking for more. There has been no action taken and we are still adhering to the original agreement with the architects.

Do I understand that
.both architects are making the same complaint?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Mr. Pearson was the
one who made the complaint, but the other architect was present at the time. As he did not say anything, I take it for granted that he is of the same opinion as Mr. Pearson, because under the arrangement each gets a certain amount of the commission.

As I understand the
amount we are now voting is towards the

completion of the building. The minister will not take it upon himself to say it will complete the whole building?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Not the $2,000,000. I said that it is estimated that we would require $10,000,000.

This will make $10,-
000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals

speechtext: And my hon. friend believes that to complete the Whole building it will require $10,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I can only answer the hon. gentleman by giving the information that is given to me that for this amount we can complete the building.

I do not believe you
can.

I see by the answer
given to my hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Copp) that $214,729 has been paid to Mr. J. A. Pearson and $40,624.52 to Mr. Mar-chand. There is a big difference between these two amounts. Is there one senior and one junior architect or are they both on the same level? What is the basis of the fees they receive? Is there an agreement between them by which one will get more than the other?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: We had Mr. Marchand and Mr. Pearson together when we made the original agreement with them on the 5} per cent basis. Mr. Pearson and Mr. Marchand agreed between themselves as to the division of the 51 per cent. Mr. Pearson, as I understand, assumed all the expenses in connection with the architects' work. There are large expenses. Mr. Marchand was to receive his portion without paying any part of the expenses.
What are these expenses?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Mr. Pearson has quite a staff of architects that he has to pay out of this 51 per cent. I do not want the committee to think that these architects get 51 per cent for their own personal services, and that they have to pay nothing out of that. Mr. Marchand would receive $40,000 for his own personal services and Mr. Pearson would receive the balance but he must pay out of the balance the expenses of his own architects and draftsmen and he tells me that he cannot afford to take the 51 per cent and do that. That is the question, but we have not agreed to any departure from the contract.
Mr. Pearson has a complete staff, I understand?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: So I understand.

How is it that the minister adds to that complete staff the different gentlemen whose names he gave us some time ago? There is the chief architect of the Department of Public Works. Why add the chief architect of the Department of Public Works if Mr. Pearson has already a complete staff?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
We thought that
as a further protection we should put on our owm architect, Mr. Ewart, and three other gentlemen under him to assist in seeing that the work was properly carried out and to audit the accounts. It is a protection all round. I think we were well advised to have all the protection we possibly could get and to put on the very best men we have.

Do these gentlemen from the Department of Public Works check up Mr. Pearson and his staff and are they getting the ordinary salaries they were drawing as employees of the Department of Public Works or do they get extra pay for the work they are doing on the Parliament Buildings?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: They just get their ordinary pay as employees of the Department of Public Works and are getting no extra pay.

There is an unfortunate condition in this contract. Practically speaking, under the terms of the contract, we are obliged to pay out the whole commission of the architects while the work is yet unfinished. I took occasion to call attention to this at a previous session. If anything were to happen to these gentlemen and the work would be still unfinished they would have the money. It is an extraordinary contract to make. If it was made by the Government it is reprehensible and if it was made by a committee of both Houses it is so much the worse.

The minister stated
that a further claim would be made by the architect for a payment of more than 5i per cent on an expenditure of $5,000,000.1 would like to ask the minister whether, if such a claim is put in by the architect, it will be considered by the committee or by the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I can only say offhand that in my opinion if there was to be any change at all it would be the committee that
would have the power to decide whether anything more was to be paid than the 5h per cent that was arranged with the architects. I think the resolution gives them that power.

The committee would
have power to make that change without coming to Parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I am only giving my
own opinion. If the Justice Department would say that the committee had not the power in accordance with the resolution we would have to come to Parliament.

Before this item passes I would like to voice a protest which I hive often made privately against the wicked extravagance which is shown in nearly all parts of this building. We have marble galore. We are walking on marble; the door jambs are marble; and it looks as if the architects had been trying to see how much of the people's money they could spend instead of, at a time when rigid economy is necessary, seeing how much of the people's money they could save. Well,
I suppose there is no use in crying over spilled milk, or uttering Jeremiah's lamentations over a too great expenditure for marble, but we can economize upon the furniture which has not yet been bought. The minister tells us that the desks for the private members are to cost $180 apiece.
I wish to protest against such wicked extravagance when the Government is in the hole that it is and cannot get the necessary money to carry on the people's business.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
That was the decision of the committee; we did not buy the desks.
, Mr. McMASTER: In that case do not ask them to buy any more desks; get a catalogue of ordinary business desks and make a selection from it. If the minister is too busy with his railways and canals, let him get the deputy minister to look after the matter and tell him carefully not to pick out waste paper baskets at $40 each. Let him look at moderate-priced desks that are good enough for anybody, and see if we cannot get something of that sort. I imagine at would be a crime to spend anything like $180 for desks in private members' rooms. The whole thing is distasteful to me; it is extravagance at a time when members of Parliament should be setting an example of economy to the people of this country.

They are preaching but not practising economy.

Mr. MeMASTER: My hon. friend from Sherbrooke says that 'hon. gentlemen opposite are preaching but not setting an example of economy. I do not know; we have not heard any great preaching of economy any more than we have seen examples of it. Let us at least see to it-and in this I believe there are some members opposite who agree with me-that we should not attempt to* have specially designed desks put in our private rooms. Any kind of desk that would suit a reasonable professional man's use should be placed in the private room for members. Speaking for myself, I do not want anything better. I would think that a desk costing one-half of $180 would, if anything, be on the expensive side. I made these remarks in the hope that no such folly will be perpetrated as the purchase of desks at the price of $180 each.

It appears to me that the criticism of my hon. friend is a little extreme. He complains of being compelled to walk on too much marble. Doubtless he is familiar with the teaching in Scripture that says "The wicked stand in slippery places."
Mr. McMA'STER: That is why I am thinking of you.

If the hon. gentleman goes down I suppose the righteous will have fallen on marble places. Whether or not there is too much marble, I think we must all admire the stone which has been used; it appears to me to be in excellent taste. I understand it comes .from the province of Manitoba and I think it is a credit to the province and to the country. Then, too, there is nothing glaring in this Chamber; I think every one must admit it is very chaste and beautiful. The desks and other furnishings are all that we could expect in the way of cleanliness, comfort and everything of that kind, and the wood is of very fine quality. I do not want to be a sponsor for extravagance, but I have had a little experience in building myself and I do not think that the point taken by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) is exactly in line with what obtains in every business transaction with architects. My experience has been, and I have built quite a number of buildings under architects, that where the proprietor agrees to vary the original contract to any extent for a few alterations or improvements-or extras, as they are generally called-he becomes responsible for the same commission as he agreed to pay on the
	.
original structure. Now, I think, that is good architectural law and is the case as far as my experience goes: That where you vary from the original contract and become a party to it-without there being anything in the contract, it does not matter whether it is there or not-if will bear upon its face the same commission that was agreed to be paid for the original building.
Do you lay that down as a principle of law?

I lay that down as an ordinary business proposition. It has always been the rule in respect to every building that I have ever had the privilege in my lifetime of erecting under an architect.
I do not think that the commission is large. I am surprised at the half per cent -at least I understood five per cent is the limit that was fixed by law. But perhaps the law has been varied to suit the times. Five per cent has always been in my experience the limit that architects were allowed to charge on buildings. The furniture does not necessarily go with the building; if that were decided on, I do not think that it was necessary to be done. In my experience the providing of the furniture is a separate thing, but if you wish to add it to the original arrangement made with the architect you are at liberty to do so. It seems to me, however, that should only be done with the consent of the Building Committee.
Taking things altogether I do not believe that the building has cost a very great deal more than was originally expected. We know that $5,000,000 was the preliminary vote; but anybody who has had any experience in putting up buildings, even private individuals, will know that house construction, especially in these days, runs to fully two prices, and in some cases to three prices, over what it did five, six or seven years ago. That is my experience and I think I live in a city where we have contractors and men who are as faithful and reasonable as they are in other cities. But I say that under existing conditions we cannot expect that buildings can be erected for the sum they formerly could. I should say, to look at it, that this building would cost from seven to eight millions of dollars. I would make an estimate of that kind myself, looking at the extent of the structure and the quality of the material and everything else that has gone into it. It may be that we are going to pay a little too much. I fancy this vote of

$2,000,000 will not finally settle the bill although I hope it will.
The minister says not.

My experience in extras and such things has led me to suppose that after you have paid for all the extras, and the extra extras, there is still something on top of that. I fear there may be something of that nature in this instance but there is no doubt that. this committee have done excellent work. Even if some members of this committee have dropped off I do not believe the Government are to blame for that. In the committee's original form I think there were more Liberal members than there are today. For some reason that I do not know- whether there was anything the matter I am not aware-some of those Liberal members withdrew. The hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) I think was one of the original committee-I never heard why he dropped* off-and I think there were one or two other Liberals on that committee. I believe the intention was to have a fair committee in the first place and I think, appointed in the way they were, they did constitute a fair committee. When all is said and done we must give them this credit: I do not believe there has been any rake-off or commission so far. If the committee have had fifty-seven meetings it shows they have been attending to the work pretty well. With such an excellent building as we have I trust it will be completed without any scandal. I hope that will toe the case. It would be a very lamentable reflection on the Capital of Canada if any doubt should be entertained as to whether all the money that was voted went into the building. Speaking personally, I have no doubt that up to the present time all the money voted has gone there, but I would advise the committee that no more extras should be taken on-that a definite understanding in that regard should at once be reached with the architects. That has always been my policy. When it came to having any extras or making any change that involved additional expenditure, my first question to the architect was to know how the arrangement stood in that regard. If that is done I do not see any reason why this building should not be properly completed and be a credit to the architects, to the builders, and more especially to the committee that have in a very disinterested way spent a very great deal of time and tried to minister to our comfort in a way, perhaps, even far better,
greater, and grander than we had reason to expect or to hope for.

I am afraid my hon. friend from Brantford has misapprehended the point of my criticism. I did not raise any question as to the reasonableness of the commission or as to the amount to which it should apply. I share with my brother members the pride we all feel in the magnificence of this building, and I am quite prepared to defend a very generous and liberal expenditure in order that it may be made a building of which* every Canadian shall be proud.
I have no desire to see the architects ungenerously dealt with; that was not my intention at all. What I point out is, that under the terms of the contract we are put in the position that the architects have received all their commission-in fact, they received it long ago-and they are from this time foiward, to use a common phrase, " working for nothing and finding themselves." My criticism is that whatever percentage was coming to the architects should have been distributed over the whole period of construction, but as it turned out they have got five per cent on the $5,000,000 *-I presume they have got it by this time -whether they are entitled to any more or not, although according to the statement of the hon. minister that is all they are entitled to. I am not making any point against the architects; rather I am calling attention to the folly of the arrangement under which the committee or the Government paid out the whole of the commission before the completion of the contract. If Mr. Pearson had been called away to his eternal home as a reward for this magnificent work, we would have had to engage another architect and pay him another five per cent instead of distributing the commission over the whole period of construction.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
It is all very well for the hon. member to say that, but he knows from the discussions which have taken place in this House that the architects and every one else believed that this work could be completed within three years. Mr. Pearson estimated what he would have to pay out to his staff during those three years, and unless he had been paid his commission he could not have met that cost. If we had carried out the policy that the hon. member has just recommended, then Mr. Pearson would have had to stop long ago because he would not have been able to carry on his work for lack of the money

necessary to pay his staff. That is the reason we had to do it. For a period of one year Mr. Pearson had not received a dollar until a few days ago when we paid him $10,000, and we still owe him $10,000 under the original contract. In addition to that commission, in my opinion he should be entitled to a commission on the furniture. The only difference between my hon. friend and myself is that he thinks we should have distributed payment of this commission over the period of construction, in which,event Mr. Pearson could not have carried on the work. We felt wo should pay him his commission so that he might be able to pay his current expenses. There is another point to be considered. My hon. friend knows, as I explained it a few minutes ago, that at the time this contract was let no one expected the war would last for three years-not even my hon. friend ever entertained that expectation, neither did the contractors-and as a result of the delays that have taken place injustice has been done to Mr. Pearson. I do not think it is fair to criticise him as my hon. friend does.

I am not criticising Mr. Pearson at all. I have not offered the slightest reflection upon Mr. Pearson. I think he has given us a magnificent monument that he, and his family after him, may well be proud of. If I have any criticism toi offer it is of the Government which permitted a contract to be entered into under which they paid out the whole commission years before the work was done. That is a simple statement of the position, and there is no getting away from it. My hon. friend says that if we had not done that Mr. Pearson could not have gone on. Well, according to that statement, Mr. Pearson must stop now. He has got all the money that is due him, and-according to my hon. friend- unless he gets more he cannot pay his staff, and therefore cannot continue his work, and we are going to be left at his mercy. I do not find fault with Mr. Pearson; on the contrary, I think he has given us a magnificent structure, and I would like him to be generously dealt with; but I think it was a clumsy, stupid contract under which he was to be paid all the commission years before the work was done.

I have to call attention to one little defect in this magnificent building. There is now on the table in front of the Clerk a nice little pyramid, which I suppose was designed by the architect to harmonize with the furniture of the

House. To my great surprise, however, I find that the names of the months and days are in English.
Shame.
At the opening of this session the Acting Prime Minister stated he was proud of the French language, and he gave us a very eloquent address in French, which every one of us enjoyed.
Hear, hear.

I would like to see the Government follow that excellent example in matters which may not be of any importance in the estimation of hon. members on the other side of the House, but which we on this side consider of some importance. Therefore I would ask the Acting Prime Minister and the Minister of Public Works to kindly see if it be feasible to have the names of the months and days appear in French on this pyramid, and so correct this apparent oversight.
It would make my hon. friend's protest a grea/t deal stronger if we could get on with an item of the Estimates once in a while.

The hon. minister in answer to my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) said a minute ago that this work had lasted much longer than w.as expected at the time the contract was made. I think one of 'the reasons for the delay in completion is the numerous changes that have taken place in the Department of Public Works. For the information of the committee would (the minister tell us how many different ministers have had charge of that department since construction on this building started?
Impossible.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I want to give credit to the deputy minister and to his staff for the great work they have done in connection with this building.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: No men have worked harder and accomplished more than the deputy minister and Mr. Ewart in their efforts to get this work pressed to completion. We have had changes in the department, but no delay has resulted on that account.
Don't tell us his name.
Could the Acting Prime Minister give me the names of the ministers and acting ministers of the Department of Public Works since we started the construction or restoration of this building?

Surely my hon. friend is old enough to be serious when there is a $2,000,000 piece of business before the House. What does it matter who were the ministers and acting ministers of the department? They are only temporary, they are in and out; it is the permanent officials who carry on. My hon. friend knows they did so when he was a minister of the Crown, and he knows they still do it. So long as we have good deputy ministers the work goes on without interruption. My hon. friend has a very interesting problem before him-
Certainly.
-and it will interest him a while longer if he will let it remain on Hansard.

I have great admiration for the wonderful memory of the Acting Prime Minister, but I think it would be too great a test even for his memory to give the names of all the ministers who have been through the Department of Public Works since we started the restoration of this building. A few minutes ago the Minister of Public Works told us the desks were going to remain as they are except thotse in the front row. Is it the intention to have a special type of desk designed for the front row, or to take the present desks away?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I understand the new desks will be similar to the present desks, with 'the exception that the front part will extend down to. the floor.

Another remark I wish to make. I saw in the press some time ago that as the country wanted to show its admiration for the great men who have been in this Parliament from time to time their pictures were to be engraved in marble and granite and placed in various positions throughout this building. Since I have been here I have made a point of walking around the halls and lobbies to discover in the pieces of art that I have found at the tops of columns and in o their places to try to find some resemblance between those graven images and our great men of the past and the present. I have even made an effort to find a resemblance to my hon.
friend the Minister of Public Works where I saw a man with the same affliction as I have-a	scarcity of
hair on the top of his head,- but it was such a poor piece of work and I have so much affection and esteem for my hon. friend that I would not dare make the comparison. Might I inquire if these are part of the glories of this building which have been chanted by the Acting Prime Minister and the leader of the Opposition? Do they really mean anything, or are they just there to make us remember that we see things as they really are,-prohibition being in effect in this city of Ottawa -and not as they are not? For my part I am far from being an admirer of men putting their tongues out or pulling faces or showing a broken cheek. I shall not describe the things. My memory is not good enough, and my imagination would not go as far in the worst phase of my life. Are they there to remind us of ancient Olympus or to prophesy the future? Are they threats against our future happiness or reminders of our past wickedness? I should like to know. I am told that they are called gargoyles, and certainly they are just as strange as the word itself. There may be artists who can admire them, but I have not yet reached that stage. As, however, I may have to face these gargoyles for a long time I should like to know something about them so that I may enjoy meeting them.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Gargoyles are a feature of Gothic architecture. I must really apologize for not having been around the building and looked them over to see if there is one that resembles myself. My hon. friend has been a member of this House for such a long time that if there is not a gargoyle representing him-
I hope not.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: -I shall be happy to draw the omission to the attention of the architect, so that my hon. friend may live in history, in the list of gargoyles. I should like the committee to pass this item, and if any hon. members desire to discuss it further, a discussion could be had when the Estimates for other public buildings are under discussion.
I have no objection, provided you do not put a gargoyle representing me.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I promise that, if the committee will let the item pass.
Mr. M. (CLARK: There-is this considerable advantage in not having so distinct a

resemblance to the original in gargoyles, that any ambitious member can appropriate his own and if he does not let any one know he has appropriated it, the gargoyle may serve for another member too.

As a Scotchman it might be expected that I would object, but in this case I have no objections to make. I am very proud of this building, which I think reflects credit on the architects from the foundation up. I think great credit is also due to the Hon. Kobert Eogers in whose term of office as Minister of Public Works the reconstruction was begun. He hails from Argenteuil, the same county I have the honour to represent. When we are discussing such a building as this, which is second to none in the British Empire, I do not think we should quibble about small matters. In my judgment there has not been the slightest sign of anything wrong or crooked about the whole arrangements for the construction of the building. My hon. friend (Mr. Keid) has the patience of Job in carrying out his plans. He always sticks to his post and never gets out of humour. I trust there will be no further disagreement on this matter. Any of us who builds a small house in a country place and hires an architect knows that extras always creep in, and we have to pay for them. Extras should be paid for, especially the architect's percentage. The reconstruction of this building has been the work of years. Mr. Marchand, I am sure, has worked hard and long hours, and I would not begrudge anything that is coming to him, not even a pension for the rest of his natural life.

I would suggest that in the central space behind and above the Speaker's chair there be placed a portrait of the Fathers of Confederation, and on either side a portrait of the two premiers longest in office since Confederation, Sir John Macdonald and the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
Mr. J. D. KEID f I will take that matter up.

When we adjourned the other evening I had 'risen to ask the minister if he could tell us what loss or benefit would accrue from the acquisition of the Grand Trunk by the Government.
