speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: It would be impossible for me to tell the hon. member what the results of the operation of the Grand Trunk Railway system are likely to be after the Government has taken over the road. Obviously it must depend on conditions, such as freight rates, crops, and circumstances that may occur from time Ito time. The Grand Trunk railway-that is the main line-has always met its liabilities and paid its dividends, but the hon. member must see that' I could not possibly give any idea as to what will happen after (the road is .acquired by the Government. I did make [DOT]a statement with reference to the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, which, of course, is being operated through a receiver. I gave to the House a statement with regard to the results of the operation of that railway during the last year, land I stated that I saw no possibility of different results during the present year if conditions should continue as they are now. If this Bill passes and we are allowed to place the Grand Trunk Pacific under the operation of the Canadian National Railway system, or, in other words, to bring the two .together .so that they may be operated with the *maximum of economy, then a great saving can be effected. There could be no economy if they continued separate operations.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I quite expected ithe sort of answer which the minister has given, and which shows just how weak is the Government's position in this matter.
The Government is buying a property at a cost of $500,000,000 and they do not know, and cannot know, where they are going to ,land with this proposition except that they are going to pay half a billion of dollars, and it is for that reason that I say, first, that this transaction is a bad one. I have .been expressing myself by saying that we are buying the property in the ordinary way and paying half a billion dollars and no objection has been taken to this method of expressing it. iBut I want to say that in reality when we are buying the common and preferred stocks, we are placing ourselves in the same position as a buyer, we are actually taking the responsibility of a buyer, and consequently we are imposing upon the country a burden of $500,000,000, and we do not, and cannot, know what the



financial result of the administration of the road will be.' The minister has said that to a large extent it would depend upon the freight rates. That is a question upon which the committee and the country should be enlightened now. The Government railways are losing $47,000,000 a year. It costs the people of this country that amount to own the railways. Who is going to pay this deficit?1 Is it the country at large or those who are using the facilities of the railways? If the deficit is going to be made up by the whole people of Canada, freight rates will not be raised and we will simply have to take the necessary money from the treasury to pay it. If the deficit is going to toe paid by those who use the railways, necessarily the rates will have to be increased. I consider this a very important question, and I would ask the minister to make a statement upon the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I made the statement the other day that the loss was $47,000,000 on the railways operated by the Government and by the receiver. I want to say sincerely that in so far as a portion of the loss is concerned, I believe it will be considerable for a number of years and I do not see how the people can get out of paying it,-I refer to the loss on the Grand Trunk Pacific, on which there was a loss of some $14,000,000. Then we have the Transcontinental railway and the Intercolonial. The losses on those roads probably amount to $20,000,000 or $23,000,000. While we have had criticism about the railroads in the past, I am one of those who believe that even if there is a loss it is a good thing to open, up and develop our country. We are getting the benefits of the products coming along these railways and they are of great value to the country.-
When we talk of the future prospects of public ownership, let me say, I do not believe it would be possible to get any private corporation to relieve the Government of the liability for many years; I do not believe that you could get the Canadian Pacific II ail way to take these roads off our hands for the reason that the liability will be there for a great many years. When you deduct that from the Canadian Northern railway it leaves a loss of some $25,000,000 in operation and fixed charges. I did not expect a year ago that we would have that loss, but we did not consider that we would have to increase wages by $19,000,000. No person would have expected that we should have to do that without getting some increase in rates. If it had

not been for that happening, the Canadian National railways would not have been so bad an investment at all.
It is almost impossible for me to estimate the results for the coming year. When on the first of January we were estimating the results and discussing operations for the coming year, I did believe that we had reached the wage peak on our railway system. But hon. members can read the papers as well as I can, and can see that there is a possibility of a further advance. *If we have a further advance the people of this country will have to continue to make good this loss on the railways. I believe all the railways will suffer to such an extent that they will hardly be able to run unless there is an increase in freight rates. The question of increased freight rates is in the hands of the Board of Railway Commissioners. I suppose there would be an appeal to the Governor in Council from a decision of the Board of Railway-Commissioners increasing freight rates. I think that the railways will try to show that they cannot get along without an increase in freight rates and they will come before the Board of Railway Commissioners which is the authority which increases or decreases freight rates. Whether this House is of opinion that these rates should not be granted if applied for is another matter. I do not know what action, if any, will be taken by the Government if an appeal should be made from the decision oi the Board of Railway Commissioners, but I did feel the other evening when I made my statement that this is such an important matter and the whole railway situation is in such a serious condition owing to the increase of wages and the cost of supplies that an expression of opinion in the House and from the country might be of great assistance in coming to a conclusion as to the action, if any, that might be taken in case the Board of Railway Commissioners decided to increase freight rates.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: If I understand rightly the Government policy would be to raise rates only to a certain extent but not to the extent sufficient to meet the deficit. Is that it?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: I did not say that. 1 said that an increase, if any, would be entirely in the hands of the Board of Railway Commissioners. The Government have not the authority to increase freight rates, and to what extent they should be increased rests entirely with the decision of the Board.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: But this may become, and it is in effect, a policy otf the Government, because the Government, I understand, has to face a deficit of $47,000,000. Now, who is going to pay for it? Is it the people at large, or those who are making use of the railway? To me it is a question of policy under which the Government will have to decide. It may toe that actually the Board of Railway Commissioners are the only authority to raise the rates, but the Government can give them direction either i directly or indirectly. Does my hon. friend pretend, for example, that the Government can pass a law to raise these rates, or declare that the rates will have to be sufficient to meet the expenses, or anything of that kind? That would have to be a question of policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: The law as it stands at present is this: The Board of Railway Commissioners, and they alone, have the right to say wljat the rates shall be on any railway; and if they should fix the rates so that there will be a loss on the operation of the Government railways, then I have to come to Parliament and ask for a vote to cover that deficit. If they fix the rates so that the Canadian Pacific, or other railways that I might mention in the province of Ontario, met with a loss, the railway companies must pay that deficit themselves. The Government are exactly in the same position. In the case of a private company the shareholders would pay any deficit which takes place. Where there is a deficit on a railway owned by the Government the shareholders, or in other words the people, must pay that deficit and the Minister of Railways must come to Parliament and ask for a vote to enable that to be done.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
Surely the distinction made by my hon. friend (Mr. Denis) between the whole people who own the railway and those who use the railway is a very fanciful distinction. Will it not be true that in the case of a national railway with the ramifications of the great system which we have now decided, for better or worse, to handle on behalf of the Canadian nation, that railway will be used practically by the whole of the people. Then in the case of those who do not travel upon the system, large numbers of them will have freight carried on it. I therefore think that my hon. friend's distinction is a very fanciful one. Of course there will be people who do not live near the National system and use the Canadian Pacific rail-
92)
way, but I should say it is perfectly obvious that it is a matter of comparative indifference whether any deficiency is met by those who actually use the road, or by Parliament acting for the whole of the people who own the road.
The minister has told us that there has been considerable loss on this system. Well that was inevitable under the circumstances. I am not so much concerned about that loss for the moment,'but with an unbounded belief in Canada and in its prosperity I am concerned about the loss to this extent-that as one of the citizens of this country, having the honour of a seat in this House and representing a Canadian constituency, I am anxious to change that loss into a gain, and I am sure the minister would regard me as a public benefactor if I were to point out the truth. I do not quite concur in the statement made just now that this liability is likely to be there for a great many years. I am somewhat of an optimist-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: When I made that statement I was speaking of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental only. I did not mean that that loss would continue for any length of time after we acquire the Grand Trunk railway and couple it with the Canadian National railways.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: I admit my hon. friend has pointed out the bad end of the stick. There is no doubt about it, whoever was responsible, that is so. He may be right in a measure, but it need not be. With the boundless possibilities of this country it need not toe; and I daresay discerning gentlemen in this House already see that I have taken one of the many roads to Rome. Now it is a very elementary principle, so elementary that hon. gentlemen will agree with me, that the only way to make a railroad pay is to make it do business. That is so with any industry. We must so conduct the affairs of this country that our railroads do business. Business is trade, and to trade fully we must trade freely. Now my recipe for making these roads pay is to try a large experiment in the way of taking the tariff off British goods. Is it not perfectly obvious that the only way to make railroads pay is to make work?-do business? My hon. friend on this side, and the minister also said calmly that, after fifty years of a policy which, according to the ex-Minister of Finance, (Sir Thomas White) made this country one

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I have listened to what the hon. member from the West (Mr. M. Clark) has said about the question of trade, but really the question before the House at the present time is a Teform in our railway administration. We have had experience of railroad management, such as it was, extending over a good many years, and it has ended in absolute failure in regard to two transcontinental lines, and it also ended in failure of the Grand Trunk in connection with the administration of its lines here in the East, the Orand Trunk Railway Company having practically gone into a state of insolvency.
We have too many transcontinental Toads undeT different managements, too much competition, too much duplication of lines, too many officials, too many canvassers for business, too many ticket offices; and the real question before Canada to-day is one of economy-how to stop the absurd wastage that has been taking place. This measure is an effort to put an end to the system we have had in the past, and particularly to put an end to the administration from London of Canadian railroads. What 'brought the Grand Trunk to grief was largely its being managed from London; what largely contributed to the success of the Canadian Pacific was its administration being centred in this country.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: I want to put a question to my hon. friend, who is a very fair controversialist. The Canadian Pacific was a success because we gave its promoters the earth to build in, was that not so?

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
Partially so; but we also gave the Grand Trunk Pacific a lot of our money and credit. What did we get for it? A $500,000,000 loss. The Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific were more or less engineered in the,old country. Now we are putting an end to that administration of Canadian railroads in London, and that is one of the advantages and one of the economies that I think will result from this Bill.
But we are also doing something else. As I pointed out before, I have always believed that the only way to get an economic administration of our railways is by consolidation, by making a monopoly of them rather than by having a number of competing lines as they have had in the United States. We have been told that the United States Government made a failure of their administration of the railroads they took over during war-time. But that is not the fact; the fact is that when the railroads were taken over it was found that they had been so badly managed under private ownership that millions of dollars had to be expended to put them into proper shape.
Now then, if there has been mismanagement in the States-and that is now admitted-there has also been mismanagement in this country. Our only resource now is to make more or less of a monopoly of railway transportation, to cut out all competition, to cut out all duplication of lines, to cut out all unnecessary officials, and to consolidate the business-that is what we want to see done. Those of us who believe in public ownership of'railways are waiting to see the new system given a trial. We have asked for it for years,, we have supported it in this House, and What we have been contending for so long is now nearly at the point of consummation.
I wish to speak for the people of Ontario. They believe great benefits will come from the Government taking over the Grand Trunk and consolidating the national system of railways. We in Ontario have been waiting to see the inauguration of that consolidation, and also, as a corollary, the consolidation of the express business of the Canadian Northern, the Intercolonial and the Grand Trunk, together with a consolidation of the telegraph systems in connec-

tion with these three roads. Once these consolidations are worked out, I believe they will lead to economies, and I think the people will then be prepared to deal with the other question of how the deficit is to he made good-if there is a deficit. I have no doubt there will be a deficit, and it will have to be met. The question has been raised here to-night whether that deficit ought to be met by an increase in freight rates, or by a vote in the Estimates. Probably it will have to be met in both ways, and while the minister has said -that the jurisdiction for the moment is in the Board of Railway Commissioners, I have no doubt that Parliament, sooner or later, will have to pass a resolution that will be, in substance, an intimation to the Board of Railway Commissioners to increase rates. That, however, will be a matter for a discussion later on. What we want to see now is the consolidation take place at once, so that an end may be put to the great waste that is going on. I see this waste all over the country. I see unnecessary mile after mile of railway that has been put down and is not needed now. The rails should be lifted and placed in new country to open it up. I know places where unnecessary trains could be cut out. I know places where unnecessary stations and unnecessary officials could be cut out, and a whole lot of economies of that kind effected. The effect of consolidation will be to reduce the cost of running the roads, thus making a saving to the people and to the nation.
But first of all we want to see this consolidation take place. We have been promised it for years, and it has been coming about gradually. Nearly every time that we have taken over another road it has been a lame duck, but I will say this for the old Grand Trunk: It- is one of the best railway assets in this country. I am not prejudicing the nation's case before the Board of Arbitration-because anything we say in this House will not be considered by that Board 

when I say that the old Grand Trunk is a splendid asset. I know city after city where the real estate owned by the Grand Trunk is most valuable. In Montreal, for instance, Ottawa, Toronto, Hamilton, and other cities and towns of Canada and along the Niagara and Detroit rivers where the Grand Trunk runs its real estate is a splendid asset. None of us has admitted yet what a valuable asset we get in the Grand Trunk. We get a lame duck for the time being in the Grand Trunk Pacific, but we already had that on our hands. The old Grand Trunk, however, is a first-class asset, and it will pay when it 
is co-ordinated with the National system. It will have more freight to handle by reason of being connected with the Canadian Northern, the Intercolonial, and the Transcontinental railways in the West, and the outlook is good for business. I admit that wages have gone up and may go higher, but the country is not to blame for that. We have to face the situation just as everybody in business has to face it, but the savings, once this consolidation takes place, will in my opinion more or less justify the consolidation. I believe that after the consolidation has taken place and the unnecessary waste has been cut out and economies have been effected we shall make such a success of the administration of the National lines that the Canadian Pacific will come forward sooner or later perhaps with a pooling arrangement between the National roads and itself. That is only a suggestion of mine, but I believe that making a national monopoly of the transportation systems of the country is the best way to get economy and efficiency. We are after economy and after efficiency to-day. We are after service, and I believe that all services should be made national monopolies and consolidated with a view to securing better and more economical service. Later on, we may have to pass on the question of increased freight rates and on the question of making some kind of pooling arangement with the Canadian Pacific, but the first thing for us to do is to get rid of these mistakes that we have been making for fifty years and the way to do that is to consolidate these systems. Take politics out of the proposition and have faith that the nation can get first-class railway men to administer these roads and run them in the interests of the country, giving us an efficient service and effecting economies.
There is one thing I would like to point out to the minister in connection with the experience of Toronto, and that is for some time now we have had the best station, we think, there is in Canada.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: Except Montreal.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: The most up-to-date station in Canada is certainly the new Union Station in Toronto. But for some reason the use of it has been delayed. This consolidation I think will bring about the use of it. We have in Toronto also the finest post office in America to-day.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: Everything is the best in Toronto.	-

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
Toronto's is the best. We have got a new station there now,

and we want to see it in use. The consolidation of the systems will improve the express service, the postal service, the passenger service and the freight service in Toronto, and in a great many other cities. Stations can be eliminated by consolidation, and unnecessary tracks and sidings eliminated, and the result will be greater efficiency and a saving to the people. The people have voted time after time in favour of the nationalization of the railways, and now want to see it put into effect. Once it is put into effect, and trade increases as I hope it will, then we can deal with the question whether the deficit shall be made up by increased freight rates or by a vote in the Estimates. But what we want to see now is this consolidation, and the mistakes of the past put an end to. There never was such a continuous series of mistakes as has occurred in connection with railroad administration in this country in the past. I hope that will be changed. I hope this Bill will go through, and that the Government will appoint this joint committee right away, and that the co-ordination of the lines will at once go into effect, so that economies may be effected. The real transcontinental road in this country is not going to be over simply one line, but over the Intercolonial, the Grand Trunk, the Canadian Northern, the Transcontinental, and then over the Canadian Northern again. We will have to cut out all the unnecessary train services on these lines, and if we do that we shall be able to show, not at the end of one year, but perhaps at the end of two, a much better service and very considerable savings. And then we. shall be able to discuss the question of rates.
I have listened with interest to what my hon. friend (Mr. Vien) has said with respect to the situation, but is there any other way out of it? We simply have to take these roads over; there is no other way out of it. We are in the mess. Somebody put us in the mess.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: Who?

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: Perhaps it was Parliament, perhaps the promoters of the roads, perhaps the railway magnates. But we are in the mess and we have to get out of it the best way we can; and there is no way out of it except by nationalization.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: That is the way to get in deeper.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: We have been getting in deeper every year and my hon. friend voted to put us in deeper. We are in the mire up to the neck, and it is time to get out.	1 : '	..

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: Will my hon. friend point to an instance when in past years before the railroads were nationalized there was a deficit as 'large as the one brought down a few weeks ago by the Minister of Railways?

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: But the minister said that this was an unusual year.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: This is an unusual Government.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: I am not going to defend the (Government; I am discussing the facts. We had deficits before; they were covered up in various ways; but they were there, and national reasons were given for them. But we are in the mire; the people of this country, and particularly of the West, want us to get out.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: Who got us into the mire?

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: I am not going to discuss that. The people will contend that this House got the country into the mire, and the people expect us to get them out. They are going to discuss, not so much who produced the situation, as the duty of their members in this House to rectify the mistakes of the past.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: The hon. member speaks about "getting out of the mire" by consolidation of railways and by pooling arrangements with the Canadian Pacific. Will he explain what he means by "pooling"?

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I will not go into that just now; I am discussing how to get out of the mire. But if we lay down what is underlying all this legislation that has taken place lately in the House, it is this, that public service such as transportation ought to be a monopoly and can be most economically and efficiently managed if it is a monopoly. I want to try another method of administration of the railways of this country. Canada has found all the money for "them; the railways have made a failure of their business, and the people, in order to keep the railways from asking for money session after session say: Now we have put a stop to that and we intend to run the railways. The people hope that the railways will be run efficiently by trained railway men, the railways being taken absolutely out of politics, and in that way they hope that an end will be put to the railway control over politics that we have had in the past. I think I have some idea what the people in my province want. They want to put an end to this administra-

tion of railroads that we have had in the past.

The hon. member (Mr. W. F. Maclean) has travelled far afield fin railroad matters, and has utterly failed to confine himself to the question at issue. Clark) answered me. The question which I asked the minister was this: Who is going to make good the deficit-the people of the country or the users of the road? The question had not been decided when the hon. member (Mr. CM. Clark) said that he was strongly opposed to the users of the road making good the deficit, and that he held that the deficit should be paid by the people. But he said also that he did not see the difference between the people at large and those who are making use of the railways. There is a very substantial difference; but for the sake of argument, if 
there be no difference between the people at large and the users of the railway* certainly my hon. friend (Mr, M. Clark) should have no objection to have the people make good the deficit, because according to his statement the people are none other than the users of the railway, and consequently it is not wrong to say that the people should make good the deficit. But such is not the case; there is a vast difference between the people >at large and the users of the railway, and I quite understand that my hon. friend, who, I believe, is representing his party tonight, should place himself on record as being against the users of the railways being the people to make good the deficit. My hon. friend has a policy of his own, according to which he contends that all we have to do is to increase the traffic in order to get the necessary revenue from these railways. Certainly this is elementary; anybody understands that if we could increase the traffic, we would not have to increase the rates. But the traffic cannot toe increased between now and next year nor between now and the next two or three years; it will take years and years before the traffic is sufficiently increased to meet the deficit, and in the meantime iwho is going to make good the deficit? We are now confronted with a situation which calls for an expenditure of $47,000,000 this year and will call for an expenditure of possibly $00,000,000 or $70,000,000 next year. subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: I would not approve of any policy that would make the Intercolonial a vehicle for the free conveyance of everybody. But the hon. gentleman's statement is by no means a fact, I do not accept his mere statement as proof that the Intercolonial did give the number of free passes which he was told it gave. If it did, I undoubtedly would disapprove of such management. But the point at issue is that when Confederation was contemplated it was agreed, as part of the bargain, that the Eastern Provinces would be linked up with Quebec and Ontario by means of a railway, and, more than that, the railway would pass through certain localities in order to afford every possible facility to the east in the shipment of goods. But it was understood beyond any possibility of question that the Intercolonial would never pay because it was not a financial enterprise. Every one knew that it would have a yearly deficit, and it was agreed that that deficit should be shouldered by the country at large; otherwise, Confederation would have been an impossibility. It would have been an easy matter during the last fifty years to wipe out the deficit on the Intercolonial, for all the Government had to do was to raise freight rates generally. By raising the rates the deficit would have disappeared, but the whole charge of the Intercolonial would thereby have been shifted to the shoulders of the people of the Eastern Provinces which would have been a piece of injustice from my point of view, and would have been a breach of the Confederation agreement. That is why I make an exception of the Intercolonial railway. But, I repeat, all other railways should pay their expenses, and for that reason I asked the Minister of Railways the other day whether there would be separate bookkeeping in connection with each line so that we might be in a position to know whether each was paying its expenses.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
classes of people who use the railway, passengers and shippers. Passengers use the railway for exclusively private purposes, * and possibly it might be wise at times to increase passenger rates. But freight rates are ultimately a charge on the consumer, because the farmer who lives far away in the back settlements has to pay an added cost on the goods sold by the merchant when freight rates are increased. If we desire to encourage exports and imports we must make the rates as low as possible in order that our producers may be able to compete in foreign markets. I agree with my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark), whose views I am generally able to accept, that we must provide for goods coming in the lowest transport rates possible when they reach Halifax, St. John or Quebec. Four-fifths of these goods have to be transported again to people in the West two or three thousand miles away, and the higher the freight rates the more the consumer in the West will have to pay. This deficit of $47,000,000 is the largest that has ever been incurred, and it constitutes a serious burden on the people.
Let us compare the deficit that has been produced by this board of management with the deficit upon the Intercolonial railway of which a great deal has been said by my hon. friend who has spoken before me. As an old advocate of the Intercolonial railway and an optimist as to the future prosperity of Canada, I have always had faith in the Intercolonial railway although I must say that the prosperity of the country was interrupted by the arrival in power of a Conservative Government in 1911, so much so indeed that three years of their administration resulted in bringing a condition of paralysis to our railways from a want of freight and passenger traffic in the East as well as the West. It was my lot to visit the West in June, July and August, 1914. I was in [DOT] the West when war was declared. On every division upon the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian Northern I found that local trains had been cancelled and that the people were waiting to see what the future would bring. The war was declared, and it has been won; and material prosperity has come with the war and we have had an abundance of freight in every direction.
Meanwhile I am opposed to an increase in freight Tates more particularly because it is in the interest of the country that this board of management, which has brought about this immense deficit, should be taught a lesson and we must put it in a position that it will exert its best ability dur-

ing the present year to reduce the operating" deficit. Of the total deficit of $47,000,000 on the operation of the Canadian National railways, $4,465,000 or thereabouts, is attributable to the Intercolonial railway of which we have heard so much, a deficit such as the Intercolonial railway had never before produced from the first year of its operation. When the business of the country was not 25 per cent of what it is today, when the population was only half of what it is to-day, when the traffic was not half of what it is to-day, we had a deficit under government operation, of a million to a million and a half, and sometimes a surplus. Still some people thought the Intercolonial was the cause of all the railway Doubles in Canada. Hon. gentlemen t speaking on this question last year stated that the sum total of the deficits on the Intercolonial up-to-date, and extending over a period of fifty years, was about $9,000,000. It took fifty years to produce that deficit, while this board of administration produces a deficit of half that amount, or $4,465,000, in one year. This board, composed of officials of the Canadian Northern railway of whom so much has been said, brings about a deficit of $4,465,000 in the first year of its administration.
If from the opening of the Intercolonial shortly after Confederation and down to 1911 the rates, generally speaking had been equal to those received by the company roads, whether the Canadian Pacific or the Grand Trunk, there would have been no deficit at all on the government road. Before the Hon. Andrew G. Blair became Minister of Railways in 1896 that railway had been abandoned by the members of the Conservative party, more particularly in the province of Ontario, who declaimed against government operation. As a result we on this side of the House had to educate'the people of Canada to believe in the government administration of this railway in the interests' of the country. Mr. Blair put the road on a sound operating basis. He extended it from Levis to Montreal, he gave it commercial value and importance, he gave it a good road-bed, he gave it as good an equipment as that of any other road; with the result that he came to Parliament with a deficit of only $1,000,000 or $1,500,000, and some years with a surplus.
It was affirmed by the last Minister of Railways and Canals of the Liberal party, Hon. George P. Graham, that if during the ten years preceding this administration the Intercolonial railway had had the same rates as the Canadian Pacific from Montreal to Halifax it would have been able to show

a surplus every year. That is well established. But now this administration, with excess traffic earnings of $12,000,000 during the year, brings in a deficit of $4,500,000 on the Intercolonial and a total deficit of $47,000,000 on the Canadian National railways. These hon. gentlemen say to the commission:	" Go on; never mind the deficit;
carry on, carry on." We have to tell the commission that such an administration is not to be compared with the present administration of any other railway in this country. Last year, while the administration of the Canadian National railways has brought about a deficit of $47,000,000, and while the Government and corporation railways were enjoying the same rates as the Canadian Pacific, that railway, after paying all its fixed charges winds up with a surplus of $22,000,000 to lbe put into the pockets of its shareholders. Twenty-two millions of profit after paying all fixed charges as against a deficit of $47,000,000 under government commission and no fixed charges paid! It is the duty of this Parliament to see that the board of management at the end of the present year shall be able to bring in a better report than they have given to the country for the last three or four months during which they have administered the railways.
The expectation of the Fathers of Confederation was that a small amount of traffic on the Intercolonial railway would naturally give a deficit but that with an increase of . business a greater margin of profit might be expected. It is by increasing production and business, as my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) said, that we can expect railways to prosper but it would appear that under this administration the more business we give the railways the greater the deficit. The very same remark was made to me a little more than a year ago by the ex-Minister of Public Works, Mr. Carvell. I was telling him that if he would only take over a railway in my county called the Caraquet and North Shore we would be able to give the Intercolonial more traffic and he replied:	" My friend, do
not give them any more traffic because the more traffic you give them the greater is the deficit they get." So, Mr. Chairman, I wish to notify the Minister of Railways that when I am blaming the administration of this railway I must say that during the period of the minister's own personal administration- during part of which time he acted for the late lamented Mr. Cochrane-he achieved better results than did the commission. For that I give him credit. The deficit on
the Intercolonial under his administration was only a million dollars, or thereabouts, while the commission's management has been attended by a deficit of four and a half millions or over. Therefore I wish to register my protest against any increase of rates at the present time. Later on if the commission comes with the same deficit, or any proportionate amount, it will be time for the Government either to demobilize themselves or demobilize the commission and appoint other gentlemen who will better safeguard the interests of the country.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I had thought, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) had explained the situation so concisely and clearly and had prescribed such a commonsense remedy that further discussion was unnecessary. But that appears not to be the case, and so .1 would like for a moment or two to consider some of the remarks made by those hon. gentlemen who have spoken since my hon. friend from Red Deer took his seat. In the first place I would like to ask the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis) what he meant when he asked the question: Should the users of the Canadian Government railways or the people of Canada pay the deficit on operations? I imagine that he meant by the "users" of the Canadian railways the people who ship freight over the lines and who travel over them and pay their fares. If he meant that the users of the road should pay the deficit-that is that the passenger and freight rates should be increased so that the traffic over the road would pay the deficit-I think he did not take cognizance of the fact that if that was done the freight rates would have to be increased in the case of the Canadian Pacific railway and the other private-owned railways. In that way the people of Canada would pay the deficit. They would not only pay the deficit on the Government roads but they would put into the coffers of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and other similar roads, millions of dollars that would otherwise not be paid. I would like to ask the hon. gentleman this question: If the Canadian Government railways were ever brought to the stage that the Minister of Railways told us the other day he hoped to see them reach-and I hope the minister is a prophet and that he will be able to bring the roads to such a successful point at no distant date-if such should happen to be the case, and the Canadian Government railways should earn a surplus, what would the hon. member for Joliette

propose to do with that surplus? Would he give it back to the users of the road, or would it accrue to the benefit of the people of Oanada? Therefore I hold that his argument, viewing it in both respects would not hold good.
I would also like to refer briefly to the statement made by the member for South York (Mr. Maclean). He said that the management-perhaps I should not say mismanagement, I do not know that he actually used that term-the management of the Grand Trunk Pacific from England, was the cause of the deficit. I would ask my hon. friend what was the cause of the deficits on the Canadian Northern and on the Intercolonial? I do not think he can claim that these two roads were managed from England, or from London, in any way. Therefore I do not think that his argument in that respect holds good. I will admit, however, that perhaps the fact that the directors of the Transcontinental reside in England had something to do with the mismanagement of the road. However, if that was the cause of the deficit on that particular line it would not be applicable in respect of the other Canadian Government railways.
I understood the hon. member for Joliette to make the statement that the deficit on the Intercolonial was due to the fact that it was a political railway, but I think he demurred to the idea that the Transcontinental was also a political railway, although the point was well made, because as was said, two elections were run with that railway as an issue. Now, speaking upon the subject of the Transcontinental the other day I said I thought it was up to some members of the old Liberal party to tell us where the $98,000,000 of expenditure over and above the estimated cost of the building of that road, went to.
I did not mean to imply on the occasion of my former remarks that either Liberal party, or the old Liberal Government, had stolen that money. It was due to the extravagance in the building of that road right through a portion of New Brunswick where it never, should have gone. I believe the money was actually expended: it went into the construction of the road or into contracts that were made for construction.
There is another feature of the question in connection -with that railway. I believe that the building of that road through a territory where it never should have been built was purely political. I believe that at that time every member from jNova Scotia-unfortunately for the Government

of the day and for the country-was a supporter of the administration, and as you probably know there has always been competition between the ports of Halifax and St. John for traffic. The members from Nova Scotia at that time were so shortsighted that in order to gain a little advantage for the Nova Scotia port they insisted that the road must be built through the centre of New Brunswick, across the watersheds of the Salmon river, the To-bique river and the Miraimichi river, necessitating the construction of costly bridges. One bridge which was built across the Salmon river cost nearly half as much as it would have cost to build the railway down the St. John Biver valley to the port of St. John, or approaching that. In addition, the route followed necessitated the tunnelling of one mountain, the making of various cuts and fills, and the construction of expensive bridges. That was done, as I say, in order to build the road ^o as to suit the Nova iScotia supporters of the Government of that time and to draw traffic to Halifax from a section of country that will never be developed in any way because it is a spruce wilderness. When I say that I do not mean to say anything detrimental to New Brunswick. That spruce -wilderness is probably the greatest asset that New Brunswick owns. If fires are kept out that spruce forest will be a practically inexhaustible source of wealth to the province. But the products of that forest will never be shipped out by railway, because the logs can be floated down the rivers, which abound in that country, at a very much cheaper rate than they can be shipped by rail. At the same time the country down the St. John Biver valley was greatly in need of a railroad such as the Transcontinental would have been. It would also have been a shorter route to the seaboard than would the route via Halifax. To prove how that country needed a railroad, our province, since that time, has commenced the building of the St. John and Quebec railroad through the territory where the Transcontinental should have gone. So when he talks of political railroads I think my hon. friend from Joliette will have to add the Transcontinental to the category. I am also afraid he will have to add to the list a few more of these Government railroads as well.
With regard to the deficit on the Canadian Government railways, I would like to know why it is that under the very same conditions that have resulted in that deficit, the 'Canadian Pacific .Bailway has been able to pay its usual ten per cent dividend,

and put more money into the betterment and the upkeep of its rolling stock than it ever has done in previous years. I think I could point out some reasons why that is the case. In the first place something like $400,000,000 of the money of the people of Canada were put into that railway and were practically given to the Company. 1 imagine the return for it was the excellent service which that railway affords us. The country, however, has never got any return in dividends, in fact we have never asked for it. At that time it was necessary to build the Canadian Pacific railway in order that the country might be developed. Perhaps some of the roads which were acquired by the Government at a later date were built for political purposes rather than for the benefit of the country, especially where they were duplicated and where the lines paralleled each other. I think, perhaps, the minister may be able to effect a saving by cutting out some of that duplication, and lessening the duplication of terminals and of managements with respect to these roads,, I sincerely hope he will.	*	,
However, when the system of rounding that corner is applied, in view of the deficit being so much greater in 1919 than in 1918,
I am reminded of the story of the li'title boy who was late for school one morning. He explained the reason for his being so late was that the road was -so slippery that every step he took .ahead he slipped back two. The teacher replied: "Well, Johnnie, how did you -get here at -all?" He answered: "I never would have got here, teacher, had I not turned round and tried to get home again." So I would like to see the Minister of Railways turn round and try to get home-again, for if he tried to go the other way he might reach the goal he is aiming -at. I sincerely hope he will be successful, and I am .sure we of this independent patty will give him all the assistance we possibly can to attain that end.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
One or two points have been brought out in this debate to which I would direct some further attention, Mr. Chairman. My hon. friend from Joliette (Mr. Denis), made an exception of the Intercolonial Railway, pointing out that it was a political road, having 'been built as a condition of Confederation. The hon. gentleman is quite accurate in that statement. Rut I would like to point ouit that the Ihtercolonial railway for most of the years of its -existence carried freight for the people of -the Maritime Provinces at about one-third of the rates charged on the privately-owned railways. It seems to me, however, that the time has come when the Intercolonial might reasonably he expected to pay its way. No charge has ever been made to meet the interest on the capital cost of that railway; the deficits have occurred -because the revenues have not been sufficient even to pay the upkeep and operating expenses. The hon. gentleman went on to say that all other railroads ought to be made to pay; that is, I take it, that their freight rates -should be sufficient to .meet Itheir operating expenses, maintenance, and interest on -capitalization; and he took the position that the Government, having taken over these railroads, must fix rates sufficient to make them pay.	_
Now, o-ne reason why I interpose in this debate is because I feel the public need to have the railway situation pounded into them. Hon. gentlemen surveying -a deficit of $47,000,000, hold up their hands in holy horror, and talk in a manner to scare all our people into the idea that public ownership is a colossal failure. Let us clearly understand the situation. If the people of Canada had voluntarily embarked upon the policy of public ownership, and had built -this -great system of railroads on an economic basis, -the argument of my hon. friend would be right. But it must be clearly understood that for years and years the public treasury has been tapped annually for the purpose of keeping up these lame-duck railroads; -and if there is a deficit -at the present time of $47,000,000, it -must he as clear as noonday that even weTe those railroads not in our hands, we would have to pay the deficit annually by way of subsidies to those lame-duck roads. Take the Grand Trunk Pacific -alone. We know how that gTeat system was forced upon the country. The Grand Trunk Pacific was unable to earn sufficient revenue to keep it going. W-hat did the management do? They simply stopped operation. Thereupon the Government was in duty -bound-forced-to continue operation or we would have had a rebellion in the country served by that railway. Owing to the colossal folly of all parliaments and all governments for the last thirty or forty years, the country has had imposed upon it a system of lame-duck railroads that would swamp the richest country under the sun. And yet hon. gentlemen talk as if we are to make these now nationally-owned railroads pay. Why, of course we cannot make them pay, Mr. Chairman. Take the Transcontinental-and I want to endorse the words of my hon. friend from Red Deer

(Mr. M. Clark) that not only the Intercolonial but the Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific also were political railways, and two general elections were fought around them. In regard to the great Transcontinental railway, I travelled over it last Friday and Saturday. It consists of 1,800 miles, and 60 or 70 miles from Winnipeg it plunges into a wilderness of rocks, and that wilderness, except for an occasional intermission, practically continues all the way through. That railway was supposed to cost the country $1.3,000,000; it has cost $250,000,000 as a matter of fact. It will never pay until the crack of doom. It is well we should understand this. The question the public will have to face is whether that railroad should be abandoned.

May I put a
question to my hon. friend? Should he not modify that statement a little bit about the crack of doom?

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
No. I do not believe it will ever pay until the crack of doom. For years, I believe, it will not pay even for axle grease. Now, is it fair to expect that railroad to produce a revenue? It was unloaded on the country not through any fault of Parliament. Parliament has had these babies laid on her lap, and if she did not support them there would be serious trouble in the country, because vested interests have been created all along the line of these railroads, settlers have gone in, new towns have sprung up, and the continued operation of these roads is virtually a compact entered into by Par-' liament-a compact which she must respect and carry out.
I had thought of proposing in connection with our nationally^owned system of railroads the establishment of a ward system; that is, that we should take the Intercolonial the Transcontinental, and large portions of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and put them in a national ward system, wiping out all the capital, because I believe, it was not the will of the people that these railroads should be built. If, on the contrary, it was the will of the people that they should be built, then the people are responsible and we should take the economic portions of our nationally-owned system and charge freight rates sufficient to pay operating expenses, upkeep and interest on a fair capitalization.
It is absolutely impossible that this great Canadian-owned system comprising 22,000 miles of railway, can be successfully operated in the public interest if we charge 
freight rates sufficient to meet interest on the capitalization, and therefore it seems to me that the capitalization must be wiped out. We want to get this idea of public ownership clearly into our heads and see where we are at in regard to it. We have embarked on public ownership, and if there is one thing needed in connection with our ownership of the system it is the education of the public as to the facts. I am not here to charge any particular Parliament or party with responsibility for this group of follies. Both parties have been responsible for these follies; the people of Canada through Parliament and successive governments have been on a railroad drunk for forty years. It is just as well, the time having come for sobering up, that we should face the facts frankly, for in no other way can we make a success of our publicly-owned system; we must have a clear understanding of the situation and of the duties pertaining to that situation.
Now, I wish to say a word or two in reference to freight rates. Some hon. gentlemen take the view that tjiose rates should be increased sufficiently to pay operating expenses, upkeep and interest on capital. If we attempt to do that in regard to our nationally-owned system at the present time, we would place an enormous burden on the people. If we increase freight rates on that system, we must increase the freight rates on all railways, and it is calculated that the increase proposed would cost this country $80,000,000 a year, but, of that $80,000,000, $50,000,000 would go into the coffers of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Canadian Pacific has been subsidized by the people of Canada to the .extent almost of a billion dollars, when you take into account exemptions from taxation and exemptions in respect to material and other things, which I have no time to go into to-Right; it has had subsidies sufficient to build its entire system, and 'hon. gentlemen should remember that by virtue of these immense subsidies that have been poured into the pockets of the Canadian Pacific in a munificent Oriental fashion, the company has been able to pay 10 per cent, not on the capital it invested, 'but on the capital the people invested in the railway, and it has accumulated and now has in its treasury the sum of $235,000,000. Are you going to impose an additional burden upon the people of Canada in order that the Canadian Pacific, which does not need it, should get $50,000,000 out of the pockets of the

people of this country, -when all we would be getting would be $30,000,000? Is it not far better to face the music and pay this $30,000,000 out of the national treasury to make up the deficit on the nationally-owned system of railways? Infinitely better, because if you impose additional freight rates the people of Canada will have to put up $80,000,000-for it all comes out of the pockets of the people in the long run. The only sane policy for this country to embark upon is to face the facts. Inasmuch as the whole people, not only shippers of freight and users of the road, but all people who supported governments and parliaments in times past, are responsible for the present situation, let them take their medicine and pay out of their pockets in one way or the other this $30,000,000; but do not let us impose a burden of $80,000,000 on the people unnecessarily.
Consider what such a tax would mean in all avenues. It would give the merchant and all sorts of people an opportunity of advancing their prices, and you cannot tell where the end would be In the present stage of the country's history it would seem to me to be absolute folly to add one crace to the burdens which the people are carrying at the present time. Tt is unnecessary for me to talk to this House about the unrest in the country and the danger that threatens the commonwealth. One of these days we will blow up unless we are able to stay the high cost of living. One way to increase the cost of living is to allow an increase in freight rates, and I think members of the Government and of this House should very, very carefully consider this point before they accede to such an increase.

speechtext:
So much exception has been taken to and so much criticism has been levelled at the expression "political road" that I want to make clear once for all that by a political road I do not mean a road that was built for the sake of a political party-I do not think it is capable of meaning that-but a road that was built to achieve a political event. Confederation was a political event that would not have been possible but for the building of the Intercolonial. I therefore say that the Intercolonial was a political road, because it was built in order to achieve a political event. That dsitinguishes a political road from one built on an economic basis. A road may be built on an economic basis, it may be built for a political reason, or for a military reason. We have no military roads in Canada, but they had them in Europe before the war. Wte cannot say, simply because two elections were held while the Transcontinental was being built, that that was a political road.
iMy hon. friend (Mr. Richardson) said that if we raised the rates on the National railways we would have to raise the rates all round, and that the Canadian Pacific would get the benefit of the increase, that it would get a certain revenue from the people of this country which it would not get otherwise. That is absolutely true. But I would remind my hon. friend that this eventuality has already been foreseen, and was provided for by the Government when it imposed a surtax of $7,000,000 a year on the Canadian Pacific. Perhaps every hon. member of the House is not conversant with the fact that the Canadian Pacific has been singled out by the Government and is now paying a surtax, over and above the general tax on corporations, of $7,000,000 a year. If that was a right

thing for the Government to do, it will also be right for the Government to say that if by increasing the rates the Canadian Pacific earnings should be $10,000,000 more, the increase shall not serve to enrich the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific but shall be paid back to the treasury of the country in the shape of such a tax as is now imposed on the Canadian Pacific. Consequently, if the Government roads were made to pay their expenses, there would be no deficit to be met from the treasury, and on the other hand we would receive a larger revenue from the surtax imposed on the Canadian Pacific.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Denis) and my hon. friend (Mr. M. Clark) have given us their definitions of a political road. My hon. friend (Mr. M. Clark) called the Grand Trunk Pacific and Transcontinental political roads because two elections were held while they were building. He might just as well call the Canadian Northern, which was subsidized for long years by the Government that immediately preceded the Unioin Government, and which was eventually bought by that same Government, a political road. If the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Intercolonial were political railways, this was a political railway; and the reason this railway was taken over by the Government at the time was that the country was afraid, having lent so much money to the Canadian Northern, that they would not be able to make both ends meet and that finally the big interests at the back of it, Mackenzie and Mann and the Bank of Ctommerce, might be forced to close their doors.
I want to say something in reference to the manner in which the Government always brings before the House gigantic problems like the one before us at present. Last year, when this Bill was before the House, I asked the Minister of Railways for an explanation regarding the position of the Pullman Car Company in relation to the Grand Trunk Railway Company. I also asked-and other members on this side did the same for a list of the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company,, but we did not get it. The leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) at the beginning of this session asked that the agreement that was to be made between the Government and the Grand Trunk Railway Company be produced. We were told that later on it would be brought down. But at the beginning of this session we did not have it. The Government brought it down 
a short time ago when they claimed that they needed to submit it to the House because there was a flaw in the proceedings that were had in England, although previously the Government had led. us to believe that it was not necessary for us to ratify the agreement, nor even to see it. Recently, there were put on the Grder Paper certain questions regarding the assets and the financial position of the railways which are controlled by the Grand Trunk Railway Company and which are to be found in the appendix annexed to the agreement. For instance, on the 29th March last, I put the following question on the Order Paper:
1.	What are the assets and liabilities of the Bay City Terminal Railway Company, one of the companies directly controlled by the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada?
2,	What were the costs of operation and maintenance of said railway for the last year?
3'. What is the yearly revenue of said railway?
i. Where is the Bay City Terminal Railway situated?	[DOT]
5. What is the length of this railway?
The hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Gauvreau) put a question on the Order Paper regarding the Canadian Express Company, another regarding the Terminal Warehouse Registered,, a third regarding the St. Clair Tunnel Company, and a fourth regarding the Portland Elevator Company. The hon. member for iL'Assomption-Mont-calm (Mr Seguin) put a question on the Order Paper regarding the Ottawa Terminals Railway Company, another regarding the Ontario Oar Ferry Company, another regarding the Barre 'Granite railway: The hon. member for Westmount-<St. Henri (Mr. Leduc) put a question on the Order Paper regarding the Bethel Granite railway; the hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr.( Euler), a question regarding the Detroit, Grand Haven and Milwaukee Railway Company. Other members put on the Order Paper questions regarding the Pontiac, Oxford and Northern Railroad Company; the Chicago, Kalamazoo and Saginaw railway ; the Chicago and Western Indiana Railroad Company; and, as a matter of fact, each and every railway .directly controlled by the Grand Trunk Railway Company and in which this company owned from fifty to one hundred per cent of the stock. At that time the Minister of Railways did, not even say: We will give you an order for return and this informatian will be brought down so that you may get a good knowledge of these roads and can discuss them fully; but he said: The information is not available at present; we cannot give you any detailed

information; you can know nothing about the matter, because this is a matter that is to be investigated before the board of arbitrators, and you aTe not going to know anything about it now. This is one thing to which I must object. We are here as representatives of the people of this country; -and when as to-day, when an agreement is submitted that' calls for our ratification, we have surely a right to know exactly what constitutes the assets of certain railways which are controlled by the main railway which we are buying, where they are situated, what their revenues are and what we may expect to obtain when we have on our shoulders this great railway and the subsidiary railways controlled by it. I am afraid that the earnestness of the Government in bringing this measure before Parliament to-day and asking us to ratify it after they told us last year that that was not neces-sary, is for the purpose of having us ratify a bargain which we are making today and which we have -said many a time -and I repeat it again-is a bad bargain. I am told on good authority-I cannot say exactly from what source, because I might be mistaken-that the -Grand Tf-unk Railway Company is at present confronted with a very serious difficulty; that in the very near future they will need a large amount of money, some people say $15,000,000 or $20,000,000, in order to carry on the operations of the road, and that the reason why the Government are bringing this measure before Parliament is so that they can say later on, if this surmise be true; Well, you saw the agreement and Parliament passed upon it.
Last year we objected to discussing the proposition of ibuying this railway without having a thorough investigation made of the same. This was refused, and we shall have to be mighty careful this time as to the way we vote, because some people might say we are inconsistent should we seem to be approving this year a measure which last year by our action we showed that we entirely disapproved. We were told that there was a certain possible error; that same eminent lawyers in England and in this country did not view the matter in the same light. We were told that some people say it might be that the meeting was held in error, while other people say that it might be legal. This Bill is brought down also to correct another little mistake, to include two or three little railways, subsidiaries of the Grand Trunk, that were not included in the first agreement, As has al-93
ready been said by certain mem-
10 p.m. bers on this side, we are willing to correct these little errors in regard to the inclusion of these railways if the errors are only clerical ones and if they do not change the amount of our liabilities; -but we object to confirming and ratifying the old agreement which is submitted to us to-day. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) has said; Well, this to correct the errors, and also at the same time we thought it would be a good thing to have the agreement ratified by the House. The people of this country, when they look at this Bill, will look upon it and it will pass in all ages as -being "An Act to confirm the agreement dated 8th day of March, 1920, between -His Majesty the King and the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada for the acquisition by His Majesty of the capital stock of the said Grand Trunk Railway Company except the four per cent guaranteed stock." This is exactly what we objected to last year, and in order to be fair and honest with ourselves, the members who voted against it last year should again this year vote against it. Much more so for the reasons that were advanced by the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. -Denis) the other day. If the people of this country had known last year, as they -know to-day, that an amount of $47,000,000 of a deficit will be placed as a burden on this country, their representatives surely would not have voted for that proposition, and perhaps a number of hon. gentlemen sitting on the other side would have done then, as they did at the beginning of this session, namely, crossed to the other side and sq,t with us.
The only possible thing that the -Government could do to aid the country in the great financial crisis in -which we are at present would be to set aside the bargain. It is a -bad bargain, as we said last year and also this year; and when we have an opportunity at present, when we see that the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company are absolutely against the proposition, and as it has not been accepted -because the Government is not sure of its standing with the Grand Trunk Company- we should certainly not press the deal any further. We should let things stand as they are, and I do not think that the Government should press the ratification of the agreement at all. I for one intend to vote against it.
Mr. COCKSHUTT; As a matter of policy is up for decision it appears to me that the present is as- good an opportunity as



any to face the situation and see if we can decide what is the (best course to pursue with regard to this big deficit of $47,000,00 on the operation of the railways during the past year. I shall give my opinion as to what action should be taken, and I know that that opinion will not accord with a good many views that have been expressed on the subject, although there are some hon. members who I believe may agree with me. I think that the public railways of Canada should either be reduced in capitalization, as has been suggested by the hon. member for (Springfield (Mr. Richardson), or, if it is thought that they are all good assets, we should seek finally to earn some dividends upon these roads. For myself, I largely agree with the view expressed by the hon. member for Springfield as to the entire misplacement of a large part of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental. That is a pail of spilt milk that cannot be regained, and there is no use in quibbling in this respect. I have always taken this view, having urged it on many a platform on many occasions, that the whole railway was badly conceived, badly placed, and we can never hope to make it up in our time. The Canadian Northern, on the other hand, is for the most part a well placed road, and though it is perhaps not in efficient condition it is, at the price the country paid for it, a fairly good asset which ought to be worth in these times of high prices one hundred cents on the dollar if it is anything like a railway placed in a country that has any hope of success in the way of producing traffic. -
But I find that a good many members of this House are disposed to argue that we should make up this $47,000,000 by making it a charge on the treasury of 'Canada and taking it out of the pockets of the whole of the people, voting sums year by year to keep the roads going. As a business man I cannot endorse that view. My opinion is that we ought to capitalize these roads at a fair price. We shall have perhaps twelve or fifteen hundred million dollars invested in railways publicly owned in Canada. If these railways are worth only fifty cents on the dollar then, if the amount invested is fifteen hundred million dollars, let us make that $750,000,000 by writing off fifty per cent for bad policy, erratic construction and misplacement of roads, duplication of lines, etc., for which we have suffered and for which perhaps both parties are to a certain extent responsible, although I think that my hon. friends oppos-

ite are a good deal more responsible for i that condition of things than we are. I know that the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) does not agree with that statement, but it is the fact. The Grand Trunk Pacific and Transcontinental were known to be political roads when projected, and it was not contemplated that they should pay at the time they were built nor in the near future. My judgment is that they should never have been built at all. The Hudson Bay Railway I put in the same category, although in this view I may not be supported by some of my western friends. But that is another enterprise for which the present Government are more or less responsible. They found it partly built when they came into power, and nearly completed it at a cost of some $30,000,000. I am told by the Minister of Railways that the contract was let by previous government, so that this Government could not be held responsible for that; but $30,000,000 has been put into that undertaking and quite a bit more will be required before it is finished. Now that these moneys have been misspent and we cannot recall them I think that is just as well for us to make the best of what remains. I want to submit that if under existing conditions of labour, fuel, cost of rolling stock and operation generally, we are carrying freight and passenger traffic at less than paying rates we are not doing good business; and to say that you can wipe out any deficit by doubling traffic is only putting yourself further in instead of coming out of your difficulty. The situation is a good deal like the female huckster selling apples at twopence a pound, who, when she was remonstrated with in the matter of price, said to her customer; "I assure you, madam, I am losing a penny a pound on every pound I sell." The purchaser asked her how she could continue to do business on such a basis, and the reply was: "Oh, well, it is the quantity that does it." Now, if we are losing a dollar a ton on every ton of freight we are carrying-and that is about the condition of things-^that is not good business by any means, and it should not be continued another year; and whether it oppresses the people or not, the people who use the railways are the people who should pay whether they are passengers or shippers. I say this, knowing that I myself shall he hit very hard. I shall be hit as hard as most hon. gentlemen and probably harder than a good many, when I advocate that freight rates be put on a paying basis.
