speechtext:
I have endeavoured to answer that question from my standpoint, which I am well aware does not commend itself to the hon. member for Red Deer. I admit that the general prosperity of the country must be considered, and I do not complain about the fact that they have carried hay free in the West when cattle were dying, although we never received such concessions in Ontario, or at least in my part of the country. I am not finding any fault with that, and the general good of the public must certainly be considered. But surely, if after having spent fifteen hundred million dollars of capital invested in twenty-two thousand miles of road, we wipe it all out, and still do not
93i
make any income and if we do not pay the operating expenses, there must be something wrong either wdth the management or the quality and carrying capacity of this country.
The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) is very fond of pointing us to the old country and I am going to take him to the old country as an example in railway matters. It is a free trade country and we would presume they manage their railways as well as they do their trade. Sir Henry Acworth says that they are continuing to toy with railway traffic and that they have been doing that for the last fifty oi seventy-five years. " Toy" is the word to use. He says that Britain is continuing to carry her traffic in ten-ton trucks the same as she did when George Stephenson first put his railway engine on the line, and that these are not more than half full, or sometimes not more than a third full. His statement is that if they fully loaded these ten-ton trucks it would give 1,000 tons for a whole train, whereas in Canada and the United States, he says, our cars carry from 40 to 100 tons per car, and that a full train load in Canada and in the United States is 3,000 tons as against 1,000 for Great Britain. Mr. D. B. Hanna has told us that, if we will give him the same rate of freight that they get on the British railways where they have no snow, ice, or other hard conditions such as we have in this country, he will pay off the national debt within a very few years. This is the statement, I believe of Mr. D. B. Hanna. British freight rates are five, six and seven times as much as ours. Our freight rate is three-quarters of a cent per ton per mile against two pence ha'penny for the British lines, and in some cases three, four and five pence per ton per mile from the Midland counties to London. I have freighted traffic from London to Brantford, 3,000 miles-200 miles of rail freight from London to Liverpool, across the Atlantic to Montreal- and the goods laid down in Brantford cheaper than the English railways were charging the Midland farmers for a 200 mile haul to London. That is a statement that can be verified. Canada is giving the people the very cheapest class of railroading that has been given in almost any country in the world. There is no country that equals us unless it be the United States. Some few American roads may equal us but there are very few that equal what is being done by the great Canadian Pacific " railway and what our Canadian National railways are doing to a considerable extent. I therefore say as a business man that it is

our duty to advise the minister in this matter. He asks the advice of'the members of the House and I am going to give him my advice. It is that the rates should be placed at such a point that they will at least pay operating expenses and that it should be done at as early a date as possible. Just as soon as they get these increased" rates in force these railways should be made to pay operating expenses. And surely if the railroads give this service at cost nobody is going to ask anything better than that. With this investment that we have of $1,500,000,000 in publicly owned railways, is it too much to ask that the people of Canada who use the roads shall pay what would be, not a return on the money invested, but simply for the labour, the fuel, the rolling stock, and the wear and tear upon the line to say nothing whatever about a profit.
I think that nothing else can reasonably be expected.
I listened to my hon. friend across the way (Mr. Casgrain) expatiating upon the wastage policy of the Government, and I wondered if he had ever taken any hand in helping to load up the Government in any way, as I understand he comes from a constituency that did have a road that was not at all profitable. I would like to know what attitude he took upon the acquisition ol that road by the Government. The trouble is that a great many gentlemen who get up and' criticise the Government; have on occasion helped to load this Government up with railways that are unprofitable.

speechtext: I suppose that in a moment of tenderness they yielded to the pressure of hon. gentlemen on the other side and took over the road, although that I cannot tell. What I want to put clearly is that the minister should in so far as he is able assist the management to make these roads self-sustaining so that next year he will not have to come down to the House and ask for $47,000,000 or $50,000,000 to cover the deficit on the operations of the roads. I think that the country will say that while they are willing to accept the loss and while they will wipe out the capital, they certainly could not be expected to continue to operate the railway at a loss in addition to counting the capital as nothing.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it was my
duty to put myself on record as opposing this measure. Last year when it was presented to the House on its merits I voted against it, and I do not think that I can now vote for the ratification of the agreement which was made under its clauses.

It cannot, by any means, be said that there is complete satisfaction with this measure, or with the .agreement arrived at under it. We on the Opposition side are dissatisfied because we think it is bad business for the country, and that we thereby saddle Canada with a further deficit in respect of railway operations. The Government themselves are dissatisfied with the conditions created; they say we are obliged to choose the least of two evils. Then too, if we can judge by the reports that have been received of the meeting of the shareholders of the Grand Trunk we con safely affirm that those shareholders are dissatisfied also. But apparently, while everybody is dissatisfied with the conditions prevailing in respect of our railways in Canada, there are three classes of people who are satisfied with the Bill, and with the agreement. The first class are those shareholders who see their shares enhanced in value by the fact that they are now guaranteed the interest on them and the reimbursement at par of their guaranteed stocks. Then a certain portion of the people of the province o'f Ontario are satisfied with the acquisition of this railway because they are, generally speaking, favourable to public ownership and too easily assume that the operation of a railway and the operation of water-power are similar. There is also that other class of Ontario people who are satisfied with this nationalization of the Grand Trunk system because they think it is a good thing to remove the management of the system from Montreal to Toronto in the interests of the latter city. The third classe of people who are satisfied are the Westerners- the grain growers of the West-who think it is in their local and personal interest that the Government should acquire and nationalize as many railways as possible. They think they can bring influence to bear on the Government so as to compel them to keep the railway rates as low as possible and thus derive a greater benefit on the sale of their wheat; and to-day we had an admission from hon. members from the West that the deficit in the management of our railways should not be cast on the users of the road, but should be borne by the whole country.
Surprise is expressed at the attitude of the people of the province of Quebec who in this instance-just as in other instances, when legislation is being discussed here or public questions are considered in the cohntry-form the soundest element in Canada and regard
matters from the sanest point of view. We contend that public ownership will not be advantageous to this country. We contend that by acquiring the Grand Trunk Railway system and its subsidiary the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Government will be faced with a further deficit, and that in the present condition of our national finances we are not justified in allowing the Government to pursue that course. We think that if we are going to follow a policy of retrenchment-as advocated by the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) and if we are to re-establish our finances on a sound basis, it is not a time for us to acquire new railways which will increase the deficit resulting from our administration of railways. Is not that a sound proposition to present to Parliament?
We are answered by the argument that the Government cannot do otherwise than they are doing. We are told that these railways were forced on us, that they are " one of the dirty babies " left on the Government's doorstep, as the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) used to say. I think that is not correct. It is not correct to say that former governments-whether reference be had to the Liberal Administration, or the Government which succeeded them from 1911 to 1917- left any " dirty babies " on the doorstep of the present Government. Very often there has been criticism of railway management in the past. I have heard the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) denounce, three or four times at every session since I have been a member of the House, the " follies," which he claimed had characterized the administration of our railways and our railway policy in past years.
Sir, we absolutely had to * have railways in order to develop Western Canada. It is true that railways were built before the traffic and before the population of the Western Provinces would justify such an extent of railway mileage. But we were in a vicious circle; we could not get the population and we could not develop Western Canada except by building railways. Without population our railways would not pay, and immigrants were pouring into Canada by hundreds of thousands yearly. We had to provide the necessary facilities to give those people access to the Prairie Provinces, and to enable the products of the West to be marketed. Who will say that the enhanced value in the Western Provinces did not cover, and more than cover, the expense that the country in-

eurred. Surely the increased value which accrued to the lands in the West as a result of building railways more than met the expenditure to the country which the providing of such facilities involved.
The Liberal Administration has been criticised as being responsible for the present condition of affairs. This charge against the Liberal Administration is not justified by the facts. What did occur? In 1903 the Liberal Government entered into an agreement with the Grand Trunk Kailway Company by which that company was to build the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, extending from Winnipeg to the coast, whilst the Government was to build the National Transcontinental railway extending from Moncton to Winnipeg, and upon completion of the latter railway the Grand Trunk Company were to operate it under lease for fifty years without any expense to the country. If that agreement, which was ratified by |two subsequent general elections, had been respected, the Grand Trunk Kailway Company would have operated the National Transcontinental railway under lease in conjunction with the Grand Trunk Pacific railway.
^ Why is it that the Grand Trunk Railway Company did not accept the National Transcontinental railway? Because after the elections of 1911 the Conservative Administration changed the grading of the line and the specifications of the terminals without the consent of the Grand Trunk Company, and when in 1914 the Government was ready to hand over the National Transcontinental to the Grand Trunk Company, that company said: We are no longer bound by our agreement, because you have not yourself lived up to its terms. As a result the Government was compelled to yield to the contention of the Grand Trunk Company. In the Drayton-Acworth report it is said:
The Grand Trunk Company have already obtained a tacit release from their contract in reference to the Transcontinental half of the original Grand Trunk Pacific undertaking.
In 1914 therefore the Grand Trunk Railway Company was released from its obligation to lease the National Transcontinental railway. In 1914, 1915 and 1916 the Grand Trunk Railway Company said to the Government: You have deprived us of the connecting link between Sarnia, the western end of our system, and Winnipeg, the eastern end of the Grand Trunk Pacific system, which connecting link was to be the National Transcontinental. We have not been able to take it over on account

of the changes you made in the grading of the railway and in the specifications of the terminals. Therefore, as the Grand Trunk Pacific railway without any connection with the eastern section of our system cannot be a paying proposition, the Government must pay the annual deficit in the operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. The result was the Government admitted the contention of the Grand Trunk Company, and in 1914, 1915, 1916 and 1917 they obtained a vote from this House to cover that deficit.
Well, Sir, whose fault wras that? From the beginning of the debate on this subject both this session and last session we have been charged with responsibility for the present conditions, which we have been told are the direct result of the folly of our railway policy. To that charge I reply: No, Sir, the railway policy of the Liberal Administration was sound, because the construction of the railways under that policy was necessary for the development of Western Canada. The construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific and of the Transcontinental was not to increase the charge against the public treasury, as the Grand Trunk Railway Company was to lease the latter for a term of fifty years and operate it in conjunction with the former. But the default of the Conservative Administration compelled the Government to release the company from the conditions of their agreement. In 1914 the Government was obliged to take over the Transcontinental railway, and in 1918 it was face to face with the alternative of closing up of the Grand Trunk Pacific, or taking it over and merging it with the National Railway system.
As to the policy of nationalizing our railways, it would be useless to try to explain or to argue that it is a sound policy. Everybody admits that railways cannot be managed as efficiently by governments as by private corporations. In every other country the experiment has been made, and never with success. After our experience with the Intercolonial railway, after the experience of the Railway Board of the United States, and after the experience of all the European countries with the exception of Switzerland, how can we contend that no matter what applications there may be of disinterested and broad-minded service, and no matter what freedom there may be from political influence, we will be able to make government ownership of our railways a paying proposition? It would be childish to believe it.

We were told two years ago that the Government in nationalizing our railways intended to have them administered by the best men that could be engaged. What has been the result of that administration? Deficits, yearly increasing. The deficits this year are heavier than they were last year, and they were heavier last year than they were the year before. And it will always be so. The Liberal Administration has been accused of giving four hundred passes on the Intercolonial railway. Can we change human nature, can we prevent political influence from making itself felt in the administration of our National railways? I do not believe so. The experience of the past should /teach us that we will not in the future be any more secure against such influence than we have been heretofore.
I come now to the question of how to deal with these yearly deficits. Two propositions are put forward; one to increase railway rates, the other to charge the deficits as a public expenditure against the consolidated revenue fund. Hon. members from the West, following the policy advocated by tmy hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark), are favourable to keeping the rates as they are at present and charging the deficit to the consolidated revenue fund. I believe that this method is unfair, unjust, and unsound. How could we charge against the consolidated revenue of Canada the deficit on the railways which is due to the fact that the rates are so low that it is impossible for the railways to meet even their current expenditure? Who is benefiting by the railways of Canada? Who are the users of the railways of Canada? To a certain extent the older Eastern and Central Provinces, but more particularly, and especially with regard to freight rates, it is the grain growers and the people of the West who are benefiting. I do not find fault with them in defending their own personal interest, but I think in this debate it is our duty to consider only the interest of the public at large. I understand that the wheat production of the West is in the neighbourhood of 200,000,000 bushels annually, and that 70 per cent of this production is hauled over the roads to the eastern ports, where it is loaded into ships and sent to the-great wheat market of the world, Liverpool, and is sold. The people of the We3t and some hon. members who come from the Western -Provinces are now asking this House to sanction the principle that the Eastern Provinces shall pay for the hauling of the
wheat of the western grain growers.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: Who has been paying the deficit on the Intercolonial?

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: Most assuredly the greater part, if not almost the whole of the deficits of the Intercolonial were paid by the Eastern and Central Provinces. Twenty years before the opening of the Western Provinces, the Eastern Provinces were paying for the deficits on the Intercolonial and the interest on the construction costs. Even after the construction of the Canadian Pacific, the National Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific was an accomplished fact, and even to-day, the Eastern and Central Provinces on account of their big valuation are paying much more than their share of the deficits of the railways of Canada. Will my hon. friend (Mr. J. F. Reid) contend that Ontario and Quebec and the Maritime Provinces do not contribute to the public exchequer in a larger measure than the Western Provinces? Will he contend that the Western Provinces are contributing to the public exchequer in larger measure than the Eastern or Central Provinces? If Ontario and Quebec and the Maritime Provinces are paying to the public exchequer a larger share than the Western Provinces, it necessarily follows that their share in the payment of the debts incurred by this country, even for the opening of the Western Provinces, is larger than the share of the Western Provinces.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: Does my hon. friend contend that the Eastern people pay more per capita than the W-estern people?

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
It is not a question of the
per capita contribution, but of -the bulk contribution to the public exchequer. If your population is scant and scattered over a vast area, it is not the fault of the Eastern Provinces. No one will contend that Ontario and Quebec and the Eastern Provinces are not contributing a larger amount to the public exchequer, not on a per capita basis but as regards the bulk of their contributions, than the Western Provinces. Therefbre, I say that the Eastern Provinces have an interest in this matter, and a very considerable interest. Ontario and Quebec have done a great deal to develop the West. Indirectly they have benefited, for it has been to the benefit of Canada as a whole, -but the greater share of the benefit has been reaped by the westerner, and he is reaping the greater share to-day. It would not be just to ask this country to pay

the annual deficit on the railways simply for the purpose of allowing the grain grower of the West to carry his wheat at a cheaper rate for his own personal advantage and to the detriment of the rest of the community^ Are the manufacturers of the East asking the western grain growers to contribute to the development of their industries except through the tariff, which we ourselves oppose, and on which we want a substantial reduction?

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
What is the difference
between contributing directly and indirectly?
, Mr- VIEN:	We are in complete accord
in so far as the reduction of duty on certain manufactured goods is concerned. We contend that the basis of our economic structure is wrong and unfair, and that it should be changed. We are in complete accord in that respect.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
Is the hon. gentleman
aware that the most profitable business, in fact, the only profitable business, of the National railways has been the long haul of the western wheat?
. Mr- VIEN: I am aware of one fact, and it is this: that the railways of Canada with the exception of the Canadian Pacific are all faced with deficits, that the rates are not sufficient to pay even operating expenses. Even the Canadian Pacific, notwithstanding their big reserves, now find their net surplus decreasing very rapidly from month to month, and they already contemplate making application to the Board of Eailway Commissioners for an increase in rates to prevent the wiping out of their surplus over operating expenses. It is an absolute fact -that the 'Canadian Pacific finds its surplus melting away on account of the increase in operating expenses.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.

Does not that explain
any increase in any deficits for the Canadian National Eailways?

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I admit that, the low rates are to a large extent responsible for the inability of the Canadian Government Eailways to meet the fixed charges and operating expenses, but so far the Canadian Pacific has been meeting its obligations with the existing rates which prevail for the Canadian Government Eailways as well.
I do not consider it fair reasoning to state in this House, as the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Eichard-son) said to-night, that we could not increase the rates because the Canadian Pacific would benefit thereby. If the Canadian [GVIr. Vien.l
railways, whether nationalized or privately- * owned cannot meet their operating expenses and fixed charges without an increase in the rates, the only sound policy is to increase the rates sufficiently to cover the deficits. This is the reason why the west-ener is particularly favourable to nationalization of railways; as I said before, they want the Government to kpep the rates low, and they think that if the railways are nationalized, through their influences on the Government or through fear that the Government might have of them-that might be putting the matter more clearly-they will keep the rates low, and then these westerners will benefit by those low rates, because of the increased profit on the sale of their wheat.

speechtext: But first and above all, the westerner himself, not only through the increased value given to his land, but through the greater facility that he has in exporting his grain and-carrying it to its natural market.

speechtext: Who were the original westerners?

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: The original westerners were, for a certain proportion of the population, from Ontario and the Eastern Provinces, but the great bulk of the people of the Western Provinces, if I am correct-and I speak subject to correction-c-ame through immigration, and these railways have been for the benefit, not mainly of those who came from the Eastern Provinces, but of the whole population of the West,, that is to say, of the immigration that came and settled in the Western Provinces.

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext: Have the railways not also been of great benefit to manufacturers in Eastern Canada?

subtopic: GRAND TRUNK ACQUISITION BY THE GOVERNMENT. ' BILL TO CONFIRM THE ARGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.
speechtext:
Undoubtedly, and that is the answer I gave to the hon. gentleman who interrupted me a minute ago. I am not finding fault with the westerner who tries to look after his personal interest; but it is the duty of members of this House to look into this matter, not from the interest of a section of the country, but from a national point of view. Moreover, the westerner, the grain grower and the farmer of the Eastern Provinces should consider their true interest, and if they think of the matter in a sound manner and seriously, they will find that in the long run this policy is going to be detrimental to themselves and more especially to their personal interests.
The country is financially embarrassed at the present. The Minister of Finance will not be able this year to find in the revenue of the country, ordinary or extraordinary, the necessary money to meet the expenditure. We shall have a deficit this year; we shall have a deficit next year; we shall have a deficit for several years to come. Where is the money to come from? Undoubtedly it will have to come through direct taxation. Last year the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) suggested that we should even tax the unimproved value of land, a first taxation on land; which will be followed, if our deficit continues to
increase, by direct taxation on land whether improved in value or unimproved. Who is going to make good the deficit, if not the land owner? Is it then not in the interest of all those who own land to see to it that the affairs of the country are balanced; that the income meets the expenditure, and that we do not create further deficits by the administration of railways through public ownership? Who will pay in the long run? The farmer, the owner of the land is going to pay in the long run all those expenditures with which we saddle the country.
